By adding up a few respiratory volumes, one can derive various pulmonary capacities which can be used in clinical diagnosis: Inspiratory Capacity (IC) is the total volume of air a person can inspire after a normal expiration, which includes tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume (TV + IRV); Expiratory Capacity (EC) is the total volume of air a person can expire after a normal inspiration (TV + ERV); Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air that will remain in the lungs after a normal expiration (ERV + RV); Vital Capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, or the maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a forced inspiration (ERV + TV + IRV); Total Lung Capacity (TLC) is the total volume of air accommodated in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration (RV + ERV + TV + IRV or VC + RV).
Given: TV 500, IRV 3000, ERV 1100, RV 1200 mL; 12 breaths min⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: VC = IRV + TV + ERV; IC = TV + IRV; FRC = ERV + RV; TLC = VC + RV; minute volume = TV × rate.
Step 1: VC = 3000 + 500 + 1100 = 4600 mL; IC = 500 + 3000 = 3500 mL.
Step 2: FRC = 1100 + 1200 = 2300 mL; TLC = 4600 + 1200 = 5800 mL.
Step 3: Minute volume = 500 × 12 = 6000 mL min⁻¹.
Why: Capacities are sums of the non-overlapping volumes, and residual volume is included only in FRC and TLC.
Why not the others: (B) IC and VC swapped; FRC and TLC wrong; minute volume ignores rate. (C) VC excludes RV; IC includes TV. (D) VC omits TV; TLC omits RV.
Key point: VC = IRV + TV + ERV; FRC = ERV + RV; TLC = VC + RV.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Counting orbitals and electrons allowed by sets of quantum numbers, radial and angular nodes of orbitals, and identifying impossible quantum-number combinations
questions.question: Consider the statements: (I) n = 3 shell can hold 18 electrons; (II) the number of electrons with n = 4, ml = 0 is 8; (III) a 3p orbital has 1 radial node and 1 angular node; (IV) the set n = 2, l = 2, ml = 0 is allowed; (V) a 4f subshell has 7 orbitals. Which option gives exactly the correct statements?
options: A) I, II and IV only
B) I, II, III and V only
C) I and IV only
D) III and IV only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) I, II, III and V are correct; IV is impossible.
Concept: Quantum numbers describe the orbitals: the principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3, …) determines the size and to a large extent the energy of the orbital, and the number of orbitals in a shell is n², so a shell can hold 2n² electrons; the azimuthal quantum number l defines the three-dimensional shape of the orbital and for a given n takes values 0 to n − 1 (s, p, d, f for l = 0, 1, 2, 3); the magnetic orbital quantum number ml gives the spatial orientation and takes 2l + 1 values from −l to +l; the electron spin quantum number ms is +½ or −½, so each orbital holds at most two electrons. The total number of nodes of an orbital is n − 1; the number of angular nodes is l, and the number of radial nodes is n − l − 1. For n = 4, l can be 0, 1, 2, 3, and each of these subshells has exactly one orbital with ml = 0, so there are 4 such orbitals holding 8 electrons. An f subshell (l = 3) has 2(3) + 1 = 7 orbitals.
Given: Five statements.
Formula/Principle: Orbitals per shell = n²; l ≤ n − 1; orbitals per subshell = 2l + 1; radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes = l.
Step 1: (I) 2 × 3² = 18 ✓; (II) n = 4 has l = 0–3, each with one ml = 0 orbital ⇒ 4 × 2 = 8 ✓.
Step 2: (III) 3p: radial = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1, angular = 1 ✓; (IV) l = 2 needs n ≥ 3 ✗.
Step 3: (V) 2(3) + 1 = 7 ✓.
Why: Each statement is tested directly against the allowed ranges of l and ml and the node formulae.
Why not the others: (A) Includes the forbidden IV and omits III and V. (C) IV is impossible. (D) IV is impossible; I, II and V are true.
Key point: l ≤ n − 1; 2l + 1 orbitals; radial nodes n − l − 1, angular nodes l.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the anomalous behaviour of the first member of a group — lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine — in terms of small size, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals
questions.question: Which explanation of the anomalous behaviour of second-period elements is correct?
options: A) Second-period elements behave like the rest of their groups because they have the same valence electron count
B) Carbon cannot catenate; nitrogen forms NCl₅ like PCl₅; Be has a covalency of 6

C) The first member of each group (Li to F) differs from heavier members because of its small size, large charge/radius ratio, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals, so its maximum covalency is limited to four (B forms [BF₄]⁻ while Al forms [AlF₆]³⁻); it has a strong tendency to form pπ–pπ multiple bonds with itself and with C, N, O (C=C, C≡C, N≡N, C=O, C≡N), unlike heavier members; Li resembles Mg and Be resembles Al (diagonal relationship); nitrogen exists as N₂ while phosphorus exists as P₄; oxygen forms hydrogen bonds in water while H₂S does not; and fluorine shows only −1 oxidation state, whereas other halogens show +1, +3, +5, +7
D) Fluorine shows +7 oxidation state like iodine because of its high electronegativity
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Small size, high electronegativity and no d orbitals explain covalency 4, pπ–pπ multiple bonding, diagonal relationship and other differences.
Concept: The first element of each of the groups 1 (lithium) and 2 (beryllium) and groups 13–17 (boron to fluorine) differs in many respects from the other members of their respective group; for example, lithium unlike other alkali metals and beryllium unlike other alkaline earth metals form compounds with pronounced covalent character, while the other members of these groups predominantly form ionic compounds; in fact the behaviour of lithium and beryllium is more similar to the second element of the following group, i.e., magnesium and aluminium respectively, and this sort of similarity is commonly referred to as the diagonal relationship in periodic properties. The anomalous behaviour is attributed to their small size, large charge/radius ratio and high electronegativity of the elements; in addition, the first member of a group has only four valence orbitals (2s and 2p) available for bonding, whereas the second member of the group has nine valence orbitals (3s, 3p, 3d); as a consequence of this, the maximum covalency of the first member of each group is 4 (e.g., boron can only form [BF₄]⁻), whereas the other members of the groups can expand their valence shell to accommodate more than four pairs of electrons (e.g., aluminium forms [AlF₆]³⁻). Furthermore, the first member of p-block elements displays a greater ability to form pπ–pπ multiple bonds to itself (e.g., C=C, C≡C, N=N, N≡N) and to other second-period elements (e.g., C=O, C=N, C≡N, N=O) compared to subsequent members of the same group. Nitrogen exists as a diatomic molecule with a triple bond, whereas phosphorus is P₄ with single bonds; the high electronegativity of oxygen and fluorine leads to strong hydrogen bonding (H₂O liquid, H₂S gas); fluorine, the most electronegative element, shows only the −1 oxidation state since it has no d orbitals and cannot expand its octet.
Why: Smaller atoms with only 2s and 2p orbitals cannot expand beyond an octet but can overlap sideways effectively for π bonds.
Why not the others: (A) The first members are anomalous. (B) Carbon catenates strongly; NCl₅ does not exist; Be's covalency is at most 4. (D) Fluorine shows only −1.
Key point: First member: covalency ≤ 4, pπ–pπ bonds, diagonal relationship, no d orbitals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting molecular shapes from the number of bond pairs and lone pairs using VSEPR theory and ranking lone-pair repulsions that distort bond angles
questions.question: Which set of shapes predicted by VSEPR theory is correct for SF₄, ClF₃, XeF₄ and I₃⁻?
options: A) SF₄ tetrahedral; ClF₃ trigonal planar; XeF₄ tetrahedral; I₃⁻ bent
B) SF₄ square planar; ClF₃ trigonal pyramidal; XeF₄ octahedral; I₃⁻ trigonal planar
C) SF₄ trigonal bipyramidal; ClF₃ T-shaped; XeF₄ square pyramidal; I₃⁻ bent

D) SF₄ see-saw (4 bp, 1 lp); ClF₃ T-shaped (3 bp, 2 lp); XeF₄ square planar (4 bp, 2 lp); I₃⁻ linear (2 bp, 3 lp); lone pairs occupy equatorial positions in a trigonal bipyramid and opposite positions in an octahedron because repulsions decrease in the order lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp, and these repulsions also make H₂O (104.5°) and NH₃ (107°) angles smaller than the tetrahedral 109.5°
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) SF₄ see-saw; ClF₃ T-shaped; XeF₄ square planar; I₃⁻ linear.
Concept: The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory, put forward by Sidgwick and Powell and developed by Nyholm and Gillespie, states that the shape of a molecule depends upon the number of valence shell electron pairs (bonded or non-bonded) around the central atom; pairs of electrons in the valence shell repel one another since their electron clouds are negatively charged, and these pairs tend to occupy such positions in space that minimise repulsion and thus maximise the distance between them. The valence shell is taken as a sphere with the electron pairs localising on the spherical surface at maximum distance from one another; a multiple bond is treated as if it is a single electron pair. Lone pairs are localised on the central atom, whereas each bonded pair is shared between two atoms, so lone pair electrons occupy more space than bonding pairs; this results in greater repulsion between lone pairs compared to the lone pair–bond pair and bond pair–bond pair repulsions, in the order lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp, which results in deviations from idealised shapes and alterations in bond angles. For five electron pairs (trigonal bipyramidal arrangement) the lone pairs take equatorial positions where they have fewer 90° interactions: 4 bp + 1 lp gives see-saw (SF₄), 3 bp + 2 lp gives T-shape (ClF₃), 2 bp + 3 lp gives linear (XeF₂, I₃⁻). For six pairs (octahedral), 5 bp + 1 lp gives square pyramidal (BrF₅), and 4 bp + 2 lp with the lone pairs trans gives square planar (XeF₄).
Given: Four species.
Formula/Principle: Steric number = bond pairs + lone pairs; lone pairs placed to minimise lp–lp and lp–bp repulsion.
Step 1: SF₄: S has 6 e⁻; 4 bonds + 1 lp ⇒ see-saw.
Step 2: ClF₃: 7 e⁻; 3 bonds + 2 lp ⇒ T-shaped; XeF₄: 8 e⁻; 4 bonds + 2 lp ⇒ square planar.
Step 3: I₃⁻: central I has 7 + 1 = 8 e⁻; 2 bonds + 3 lp ⇒ linear.
Why: Shapes describe the positions of atoms only, while lone pairs fix where those atoms can sit.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores lone pairs. (B) Shapes misassigned. (C) Electron-pair geometries quoted instead of molecular shapes; I₃⁻ is linear.
Key point: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp; lone pairs equatorial in tbp, trans in octahedral.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Assigning hybridisation including d-orbital participation (sp3d, sp3d2, dsp2, d2sp3) to central atoms and relating it to geometry and magnetic behaviour
questions.question: Which matching of species with hybridisation and geometry is correct?
options: A) PCl₅ — sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal (axial bonds longer than equatorial because of greater repulsion); SF₆ — sp³d², octahedral; [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ — dsp², square planar (inner d orbital used); [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ — d²sp³, octahedral inner-orbital complex; BeCl₂ — sp, linear; BF₃ — sp², trigonal planar
B) PCl₅ — sp³, tetrahedral; SF₆ — sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal
C) [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ — sp³, tetrahedral; BF₃ — sp³, pyramidal
D) All axial and equatorial P–Cl bonds in PCl₅ are equal; SF₆ uses sp³ hybridisation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Each species is matched with its correct hybridisation and geometry.
Concept: Hybridisation is the process of intermixing of the orbitals of slightly different energies so as to redistribute their energies, resulting in the formation of a new set of orbitals of equivalent energies and shape; the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals that get hybridised. Elements of the third period contain d orbitals in addition to s and p orbitals; the energy of the 3d orbitals is comparable to the energy of the 3s and 3p orbitals, so 3d orbitals can take part in hybridisation. In PCl₅ the ground-state configuration of P is [Ne]3s²3p³; in the excited state one 3s electron is promoted to a 3d orbital, and the five orbitals (one s, three p, one d) hybridise to give five sp³d hybrid orbitals directed towards the corners of a trigonal bipyramid; three P–Cl bonds lie in one plane at 120° (equatorial) and two (axial) lie one above and one below at 90° to the plane; because the axial bond pairs suffer more repulsive interaction from the equatorial bond pairs, the axial bonds are slightly longer and hence slightly weaker than the equatorial bonds, which makes PCl₅ more reactive. In SF₆ the central sulphur has the ground-state configuration [Ne]3s²3p⁴; in the excited state the six orbitals (one 3s, three 3p and two 3d) are singly occupied and hybridise to form six new sp³d² hybrid orbitals projected towards the six corners of a regular octahedron. In coordination compounds, inner d orbitals (n − 1)d can also be used: in [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺, Co³⁺ (3d⁶) pairs its electrons under the strong-field ligands and uses two 3d, one 4s and three 4p orbitals (d²sp³) — an inner-orbital, low-spin, diamagnetic octahedral complex; in [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻, Ni²⁺ (3d⁸) pairs its electrons and uses one 3d, one 4s and two 4p orbitals (dsp²), giving a square planar diamagnetic complex.
Why: The number of electron domains determines how many hybrid orbitals are needed and hence which d orbitals join.
Why not the others: (B) PCl₅ is sp³d and SF₆ sp³d². (C) [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is dsp² square planar; BF₃ is sp² planar. (D) Axial bonds are longer; SF₆ is sp³d².
Key point: 5 domains sp³d (tbp); 6 sp³d² or d²sp³ (octahedral); dsp² square planar.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the sign of entropy change for physical and chemical processes and calculating entropy change of a phase transition from its enthalpy and temperature
questions.question: The enthalpy of fusion of ice is 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K, and the enthalpy of vaporisation of water is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 373 K. Find ΔS for melting and vaporisation of 1 mol, and pick the correct prediction of signs for: (i) N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g), (ii) 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), (iii) crystallisation of sugar from solution.
options: A) ΔSfus = 22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔSvap = 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; signs (i) +, (ii) −, (iii) −; ΔSvap ≫ ΔSfus because the gas phase is far more disordered than the liquid
B) ΔSfus = 0.022 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔSvap = 0.109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; signs (i) −, (ii) +, (iii) +
C) ΔSfus = 1638 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔSvap = 15 181 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; all signs positive
D) ΔSfus = 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔSvap = 22 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; signs (i) +, (ii) +, (iii) −
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ΔSfus ≈ 22.0, ΔSvap ≈ 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; signs +, −, −.
Concept: Entropy is a measure of the degree of randomness or disorder in the system; the greater the disorder in an isolated system, the higher is the entropy; as far as a chemical reaction is concerned, this entropy change can be attributed to rearrangement of atoms or ions from one pattern in the reactants to another (in the products). If the structure of the products is very much disordered than that of the reactants, there will be a resultant increase in entropy. A crystalline solid state is the state of lowest entropy (most ordered), and the gaseous state is the state of highest entropy. For a reversible process at temperature T, the entropy change is ΔS = qrev/T; for a phase transition at its transition temperature, which occurs reversibly at constant pressure, qrev = ΔH, so ΔS = ΔHtrans/T. Reactions in which the number of moles of gas increases usually have positive ΔS, while those in which the number of gas moles decreases have negative ΔS; processes that create order, such as crystallisation, have negative ΔS.
Given: ΔHfus = 6000 J mol⁻¹ at 273 K; ΔHvap = 40 700 J mol⁻¹ at 373 K.
Formula/Principle: ΔS = ΔHtrans/Ttrans.
Step 1: ΔSfus = 6000/273 = 22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: ΔSvap = 40 700/373 = 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Step 3: (i) 1 → 2 mol gas: +; (ii) 3 → 2 mol gas: −; (iii) solution → crystal: −.
Why: Vaporisation increases disorder far more than melting, and gas mole changes decide the sign for gaseous reactions.
Why not the others: (B) Units slip by 1000 and signs reversed. (C) Multiplied instead of divided by T. (D) Values swapped; (ii) reduces gas moles.
Key point: ΔS = ΔH/T at transition; Δn(gas) > 0 ⇒ ΔS > 0.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Deciding spontaneity from the signs of ΔH and ΔS using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, finding the crossover temperature, and relating ΔG° to the equilibrium constant
questions.question: For a reaction ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +160 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (e.g., CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂). Find ΔG° at 298 K, the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous, and the sign of log K at 298 K. Which statement is also correct?
options: A) ΔG° = −47.7 kJ; spontaneous at all temperatures; log K > 0
B) ΔG° = +130 kJ mol⁻¹; non-spontaneous above 1112 K; log K > 0
C) ΔG° = +178 kJ; T = 1.11 K; log K = 0

D) ΔG° = 178 − 298(0.160) = +130.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (non-spontaneous at 298 K); spontaneous above T = ΔH/ΔS ≈ 1112 K; log K = −ΔG°/(2.303RT) < 0 so K ≪ 1 at 298 K; when ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 a reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures, and when ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0 it is non-spontaneous at all temperatures
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ΔG° ≈ +130 kJ mol⁻¹; spontaneous above ≈ 1112 K; K ≪ 1 at 298 K.
Concept: For a process at constant temperature and pressure, the Gibbs energy change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is the criterion of spontaneity: if ΔG is negative the process is spontaneous, if positive it is non-spontaneous, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0. The two terms compete: the enthalpy term ΔH and the entropy term TΔS. When ΔH is negative and ΔS positive, ΔG is always negative and the reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures; when ΔH is positive and ΔS negative, ΔG is always positive and the reaction is non-spontaneous at all temperatures; when both are positive, the reaction becomes spontaneous at high temperature (when TΔS > ΔH); when both are negative, it is spontaneous at low temperature. The standard Gibbs energy change is related to the equilibrium constant by ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.303RT log K; a large negative ΔG° means K ≫ 1 (products favoured), and a large positive ΔG° means K ≪ 1.
Given: ΔH° = 178 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = 0.160 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T = 298 K.
Formula/Principle: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; Tcross = ΔH°/ΔS°; ΔG° = −2.303RT log K.
Step 1: TΔS° = 298 × 0.160 = 47.7 kJ ⇒ ΔG° = 178 − 47.7 = +130.3 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: Tcross = 178/0.160 = 1112.5 K.
Step 3: log K = −130 300/(2.303 × 8.314 × 298) ≈ −22.8 ⇒ K ≈ 10⁻²³.
Why: An endothermic reaction driven by entropy needs a high temperature for TΔS to outweigh ΔH.
Why not the others: (A) Sign of ΔG wrong. (B) Spontaneous above 1112 K; log K < 0. (C) Ignores TΔS; units mixed.
Key point: ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 ⇒ spontaneous above ΔH/ΔS; ΔG° > 0 ⇒ K < 1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating buffer pH with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, the change on adding a small amount of strong acid, and the composition of acidic and basic buffers
questions.question: A buffer is made with 0.20 mol CH₃COOH and 0.20 mol CH₃COONa in 1.0 L (pKa = 4.74). Find its pH and the pH after adding 0.010 mol HCl (volume unchanged). Which statement about buffers is also correct?
options: A) pH 4.74; after HCl pH 2.00; a buffer of NH₄OH + NH₄Cl is acidic

B) pH 4.74; after HCl pH = 4.74 + log(0.19/0.21) = 4.70 — a change of only 0.04, because added H⁺ is consumed by CH₃COO⁻ to form weakly ionised CH₃COOH; a basic buffer such as NH₄OH + NH₄Cl obeys pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base]); buffer capacity is greatest when [salt] = [acid], i.e. pH = pKa
C) pH 7.00; after HCl pH 6.96
D) pH 9.26; after HCl pH 9.22; buffer capacity is greatest when the acid is in large excess
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) pH 4.74 → 4.70 after HCl; basic buffer equation and maximum capacity correctly stated.
Concept: Many body fluids, e.g. blood or urine, have definite pH and any deviation in their pH indicates malfunctioning of the body; the solutions which resist change in pH on dilution or with the addition of small amounts of acid or alkali are called buffer solutions. A mixture of acetic acid and sodium acetate acts as a buffer solution around pH 4.75, and a mixture of ammonium chloride and ammonium hydroxide acts as a buffer around pH 9.25. For an acidic buffer, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; taking the negative logarithm, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pKa + log([conjugate base, salt]/[acid]); this is the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation. If the concentrations of acid and its conjugate base are equal, pH = pKa. For a basic buffer, pOH = pKb + log([conjugate acid, BH⁺]/[base]); pKa + pKb = pKw = 14. When a small amount of strong acid is added to an acetate buffer, the H⁺ ions combine with acetate ions to form undissociated acetic acid; when a strong base is added, the OH⁻ ions react with acetic acid to form water and acetate; in either case the ratio changes only slightly, so the pH changes very little.
Given: [HA] = [A⁻] = 0.20 M; 0.010 mol H⁺ added.
Formula/Principle: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Step 1: Initial pH = 4.74 + log 1 = 4.74.
Step 2: A⁻ + H⁺ → HA: A⁻ = 0.19, HA = 0.21 M.
Step 3: pH = 4.74 + log(0.905) = 4.74 − 0.043 = 4.70.
Why: The conjugate base absorbs added H⁺, so only the ratio — not the free H⁺ — changes, and only slightly.
Why not the others: (A) Without a buffer 0.010 M HCl gives pH 2, but here the acetate absorbs it; NH₄OH/NH₄Cl is basic. (C) An acetate buffer is not neutral. (D) That is the ammonia buffer region; capacity peaks at equal concentrations.
Key point: pH = pKa + log(salt/acid); small change on adding acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Relating molar solubility to Ksp for salts of different stoichiometry, comparing solubilities, and predicting precipitation from the ionic product
questions.question: Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and of Ag₂CrO₄ is 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Find the molar solubility of each in water and say which is more soluble. If equal volumes of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M AgNO₃ and 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M NaCl are mixed, will AgCl precipitate?
options: A) AgCl 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ M; Ag₂CrO₄ 1.1 × 10⁻¹² M; AgCl more soluble; no precipitate
B) AgCl 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M; Ag₂CrO₄ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ M; AgCl more soluble; no precipitate

C) AgCl 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M; Ag₂CrO₄ (Ksp = 4s³) 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M, so Ag₂CrO₄ is more soluble despite its smaller Ksp; after mixing [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M, ionic product = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ > Ksp, so AgCl precipitates — Ksp values can be compared directly only for salts of the same formula type
D) Both have the same solubility; ionic product 4.0 × 10⁻⁸ < Ksp so no precipitate
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) s(AgCl) = 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M; s(Ag₂CrO₄) = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M (more soluble); AgCl precipitates.
Concept: A sparingly soluble salt in equilibrium with its saturated solution, such as BaSO₄(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq), has an equilibrium constant Ksp = [Ba²⁺][SO₄²⁻], called the solubility product constant; for a salt MₓXᵧ with molar solubility S, Ksp = (xS)ˣ(yS)ʸ = xˣyʸS⁽ˣ⁺ʸ⁾. Thus for AB-type salts Ksp = S², and for A₂B-type salts Ksp = 4S³. When the ionic product Qsp (calculated with the actual concentrations, not necessarily at equilibrium) of a salt exceeds Ksp, the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs; if Qsp < Ksp the solution is unsaturated and no precipitate forms. Because the relation between Ksp and S depends on the stoichiometry, a smaller Ksp does not necessarily mean a smaller solubility when salts of different formula types are compared.
Given: Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰; Ksp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹²; concentrations halve on mixing.
Formula/Principle: AB: Ksp = S²; A₂B: Ksp = 4S³; precipitate if Qsp > Ksp.
Step 1: S(AgCl) = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Step 2: S(Ag₂CrO₄) = (1.1 × 10⁻¹²/4)^(1/3) = (2.75 × 10⁻¹³)^(1/3) = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Step 3: Qsp = (1.0 × 10⁻⁴)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ > 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ ⇒ precipitate.
Why: Solubility depends on Ksp through the formula's stoichiometry, and precipitation depends on whether Qsp exceeds Ksp.
Why not the others: (A) Ksp is not the solubility. (B) Ag₂CrO₄ solubility miscalculated. (D) Solubilities differ; Qsp > Ksp.
Key point: AB: S = √Ksp; A₂B: S = (Ksp/4)^(1/3); Qsp > Ksp ⇒ precipitate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Classifying species as electrophiles or nucleophiles, identifying the site of attack, and recognising homolytic and heterolytic bond cleavage
questions.question: Consider the species: OH⁻, NH₃, H₂O, CN⁻, BF₃, AlCl₃, NO₂⁺, carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺, and the carbonyl carbon of >C=O. Which classification is correct?
options: A) Electrophiles: OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃; nucleophiles: BF₃, NO₂⁺
B) All neutral species are nucleophiles and all charged species are electrophiles

C) Nucleophiles (electron-rich, donate an electron pair): OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O; electrophiles (electron-deficient, accept an electron pair): BF₃, AlCl₃, NO₂⁺, (CH₃)₃C⁺ and the carbonyl carbon; heterolytic cleavage leaves both bonding electrons on one fragment giving ions (carbocations, carbanions), whereas homolytic cleavage gives one electron to each fragment, forming free radicals, favoured by heat or light
D) BF₃ is a nucleophile because fluorine has lone pairs; NO₂⁺ is a nucleophile
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O are nucleophiles; BF₃, AlCl₃, NO₂⁺, carbocation and carbonyl carbon are electrophiles.
Concept: A covalent bond can get cleaved either by heterolytic cleavage or by homolytic cleavage; in heterolytic cleavage, the bond breaks in such a fashion that the shared pair of electrons remains with one of the fragments, giving a species with a sextet of electrons and a positive charge on carbon (a carbocation) or a carbanion with a negative charge; in homolytic cleavage, one of the electrons of the shared pair in a covalent bond goes with each of the bonded atoms, so the neutral chemical species formed, which contain an unpaired electron, are called free radicals, and homolytic cleavage occurs in the presence of heat or light. A reagent that brings an electron pair is called a nucleophile (Nu:), i.e., nucleus seeking, and the reaction is then called nucleophilic; a reagent that takes away an electron pair is called an electrophile (E⁺), i.e., electron seeking, and the reaction is called electrophilic. During a polar organic reaction, a nucleophile attacks an electrophilic centre of the substrate, which is a specific atom or part of the electrophile that is electron deficient; similarly, the electrophiles attack at nucleophilic centres, which are the electron-rich centres of the substrate. Examples of nucleophiles are the negatively charged ions with a lone pair of electrons such as hydroxide (HO⁻), cyanide (NC⁻) ions and carbanions (R₃C:⁻); neutral molecules such as H₂Ö: and R₃N: (amines) can also act as nucleophiles due to the presence of lone pairs. Examples of electrophiles include carbocations (⁺CH₃) and neutral molecules having functional groups like the carbonyl group (>C=O) or alkyl halides (R₃C–X, X = halogen); the carbon atom of the carbonyl group or of an alkyl halide is electron-deficient because of the more electronegative oxygen or halogen. Lewis acids such as BF₃ and AlCl₃ have an incomplete octet and accept electron pairs, so they are electrophiles; the nitronium ion NO₂⁺ is the electrophile in nitration.
Why: Electron-pair donors are nucleophiles and electron-pair acceptors are electrophiles, regardless of overall charge.
Why not the others: (A) Roles reversed. (B) Neutral BF₃ is an electrophile and neutral NH₃ a nucleophile. (D) BF₃ has an incomplete octet; NO₂⁺ is an electrophile.
Key point: Nucleophile donates a pair; electrophile accepts one; heterolysis → ions, homolysis → radicals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Balancing complete combustion of an alkane to find oxygen required, and identifying methods of preparing alkanes (Wurtz, decarboxylation, Kolbe) and products of pyrolysis
questions.question: For complete combustion of 1 mol propane, how many moles of O₂ are needed and how many moles of CO₂ form? Which preparation and reaction statements are also correct?
options: A) 3 mol O₂, 3 mol CO₂; Wurtz reaction of CH₃Br gives methane
B) 7 mol O₂, 4 mol CO₂; decarboxylation of sodium propanoate gives propane
C) 5 mol O₂, 4 mol CO₂; Kolbe electrolysis of sodium ethanoate gives methane

D) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O, so 5 mol O₂ and 3 mol CO₂; Wurtz reaction (2RX + 2Na in dry ether) gives a symmetrical alkane with twice the carbon atoms (CH₃Br → ethane); heating sodium ethanoate with soda lime gives methane (one carbon fewer); Kolbe electrolysis of sodium ethanoate gives ethane at the anode; pyrolysis (cracking) of higher alkanes at about 773 K over Pt, Pd or Ni gives a mixture of lower alkanes and alkenes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5 mol O₂, 3 mol CO₂; Wurtz, decarboxylation, Kolbe and pyrolysis correctly described.
Concept: Alkanes on heating in the presence of air or dioxygen are completely oxidised to carbon dioxide and water with the evolution of large amounts of heat; the general combustion equation for any alkane is CnH2n+2 + (3n + 1)/2 O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O. Alkyl halides on treatment with sodium metal in dry ethereal (free from moisture) solution give higher alkanes; this reaction is known as the Wurtz reaction and is used for the preparation of higher alkanes containing an even number of carbon atoms, e.g., CH₃Br + 2Na + BrCH₃ → CH₃–CH₃ + 2NaBr. Sodium salts of carboxylic acids on heating with soda lime (a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide) give alkanes containing one carbon atom less than the carboxylic acid; this process of elimination of carbon dioxide from a carboxylic acid is known as decarboxylation, e.g., CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃ (CaO, Δ). Kolbe's electrolytic method: an aqueous solution of sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid on electrolysis gives an alkane containing an even number of carbon atoms at the anode, e.g., 2CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + 2H₂O → CH₃–CH₃ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH; methane cannot be prepared by this method. Higher alkanes on heating to higher temperature decompose into lower alkanes, alkenes, etc.; such a decomposition reaction into smaller fragments by the application of heat is called pyrolysis or cracking, e.g., hexane heated to 773 K in the presence of platinum, palladium or nickel gives a mixture of lower alkanes and alkenes.
Given: Propane, n = 3.
Formula/Principle: CnH2n+2 + (3n + 1)/2 O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O.
Step 1: (3 × 3 + 1)/2 = 5 mol O₂.
Step 2: CO₂ = 3 mol; H₂O = 4 mol.
Step 3: Check O: 5 × 2 = 10 = 3 × 2 + 4 ✓.
Why: Balancing C, then H, then O gives the oxygen demand; each preparation changes the carbon count in a characteristic way.
Why not the others: (A) O₂ and product wrong. (B) O₂ count wrong; sodium propanoate gives ethane. (C) CO₂ count wrong; Kolbe gives ethane.
Key point: O₂ = (3n + 1)/2; Wurtz doubles carbons; soda-lime removes one; Kolbe gives even alkanes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying alkenes that show geometrical isomerism, comparing dipole moments and melting points of cis and trans isomers, and preparing alkenes by partial hydrogenation and dehydration
questions.question: Which statement about geometrical isomerism and preparation of alkenes is correct?
options: A) But-1-ene and 2-methylpropene show geometrical isomerism

B) Geometrical isomerism requires each doubly bonded carbon to carry two different groups, so but-2-ene shows cis and trans forms while but-1-ene does not; cis-but-2-ene is polar while trans is nearly non-polar, and trans isomers usually have higher melting points due to better packing; partial reduction of alkynes with Lindlar's catalyst (Pd on CaCO₃ poisoned with quinoline) gives cis-alkenes while Na in liquid NH₃ gives trans-alkenes; alcohols dehydrate with concentrated H₂SO₄ to give alkenes, and alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH undergo β-elimination (dehydrohalogenation)
C) Trans-but-2-ene has a larger dipole moment than cis; Lindlar's catalyst gives trans-alkenes
D) Alcoholic KOH converts alkyl halides into alcohols; Na/NH₃ reduces alkynes to alkanes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Condition for geometrical isomerism, polarity and melting points, and preparation methods correctly stated.
Concept: Doubly bonded carbon atoms have to satisfy the remaining two valences by joining with two atoms or groups; if the two atoms or groups attached to each carbon atom are different, they can be represented by YXC=CXY-type formulas, which can exist in two forms — the form in which the two identical atoms or groups lie on the same side of the double bond is called the cis isomer, and the other form in which identical atoms or groups lie on opposite sides is called the trans isomer; the cis and trans isomers have different physical properties because the rotation about the carbon-carbon double bond is restricted. Cis-but-2-ene has a dipole moment of 0.33 D, whereas the dipole moment of trans-but-2-ene is almost zero, or trans-but-2-ene is non-polar, because in the trans form the two methyl groups are on opposite sides and the dipole moments of the C–CH₃ bonds cancel. In the case of solids, it is observed that the trans isomer has a higher melting point than the cis form, because it is more symmetrical and packs better in the crystal lattice. Alkynes on partial reduction with a calculated amount of dihydrogen in the presence of palladised charcoal partially deactivated with poisons like sulphur compounds or quinoline give alkenes; partially deactivated palladised charcoal is known as Lindlar's catalyst, and alkenes thus obtained have cis geometry; however, alkynes on reduction with sodium in liquid ammonia form trans alkenes. Alkyl halides (R–X) on heating with alcoholic potash (potassium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol, say ethanol) eliminate one molecule of halogen acid to form alkenes; this reaction is known as dehydrohalogenation, i.e., removal of halogen acid, an example of β-elimination since a hydrogen atom is eliminated from the β-carbon atom. Alcohols on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid form alkenes with the elimination of one water molecule (acidic dehydration).
Why: Restricted rotation about C=C allows distinct cis and trans arrangements only when each carbon carries two different groups.
Why not the others: (A) Each has a carbon carrying two identical groups. (C) The cis form is polar; Lindlar gives cis. (D) Alcoholic KOH eliminates; Na/NH₃ gives trans-alkenes.
Key point: Geometrical isomerism needs two different groups on each C=C carbon; Lindlar → cis, Na/NH₃ → trans.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating boiling-point elevation and freezing-point depression of aqueous solutions of a non-electrolyte and an electrolyte using the van't Hoff factor, and finding molar mass from ΔTf
questions.question: For water Kb = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹ and Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. Find (i) the boiling point of a solution of 18 g glucose (M = 180) in 500 g water, (ii) the freezing point of 0.10 molal NaCl solution assuming complete dissociation, and (iii) the molar mass of a non-volatile non-electrolyte if 2.0 g in 100 g water lowers the freezing point by 0.372 K.
options: A) 373.104 K (ΔTb = 0.104 K); 272.628 K (ΔTf = 0.372 K, i = 2); 100 g mol⁻¹; colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, so electrolytes show abnormal values corrected by the van't Hoff factor i
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 373.104 K; 272.628 K; 100 g mol⁻¹.
Concept: The boiling point of a solution is always higher than that of the pure solvent in which the solution has been prepared, because the vapour pressure of the solvent decreases in the presence of a non-volatile solute and the solution must be heated more to reach atmospheric pressure; experiments have shown that for dilute solutions the elevation of boiling point (ΔTb) is directly proportional to the molal concentration of the solute: ΔTb = Kb m, where Kb is the boiling point elevation constant or molal elevation constant (ebullioscopic constant). The lowering of vapour pressure of a solution causes a lowering of the freezing point compared to that of the pure solvent; for dilute solutions, the depression of freezing point (ΔTf) is directly proportional to molality: ΔTf = Kf m, where Kf is the freezing point depression constant or molal depression constant (cryoscopic constant). Since ΔTf depends on the number of moles, molar mass can be found from M₂ = (Kf × w₂ × 1000)/(ΔTf × w₁). When ionic compounds dissolve in water they dissociate into ions; for example KCl gives K⁺ and Cl⁻, so 1 mol of KCl gives 2 mol of particles and the colligative property is about twice the expected value; to account for the extent of dissociation or association, van't Hoff introduced a factor i, defined as normal molar mass/abnormal molar mass, or the total number of moles of particles after dissociation/association divided by the number of moles before; the equations become ΔTb = iKb m and ΔTf = iKf m.
Given: Pure water boils at 373.00 K and freezes at 273.00 K; (i) 0.10 mol glucose in 0.500 kg; (ii) m = 0.10, i = 2; (iii) w₂ = 2.0 g, w₁ = 100 g, ΔTf = 0.372 K.
Formula/Principle: ΔTb = iKb m; ΔTf = iKf m; M₂ = Kf w₂ 1000/(ΔTf w₁).
Step 1: m = 0.10/0.500 = 0.20 ⇒ ΔTb = 0.52 × 0.20 = 0.104 K ⇒ 373.104 K.
Step 2: ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 0.10 = 0.372 K ⇒ Tf = 273.00 − 0.372 = 272.628 K.
Step 3: M₂ = (1.86 × 2.0 × 1000)/(0.372 × 100) = 100 g mol⁻¹.
Why: Colligative properties count particles, so NaCl doubles the effect of a non-electrolyte of the same molality.
Why not the others: (B) Uses Kb directly as ΔTb; i ignored; molar mass halved. (C) Molality and i wrong; molar mass doubled. (D) Signs reversed; molar mass wrong.
Key point: ΔTb = iKb m; ΔTf = iKf m; i = 2 for NaCl.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating ΔG° and the equilibrium constant of a galvanic cell from its standard EMF and relating the signs of E°, ΔG° and K
questions.question: For the Daniell cell Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s), E°cell = 1.10 V (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹). Find ΔG° and log K at 298 K, and pick the correct statement.
options: A) ΔG° = −106 kJ mol⁻¹; log K = 18.6; E° > 0 means non-spontaneous
B) ΔG° = +212 kJ mol⁻¹; log K = −37.3

C) ΔG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96 500 × 1.10 = −212.3 kJ mol⁻¹; log K = nE°/0.059 = 2 × 1.10/0.059 ≈ 37.3, so K ≈ 2 × 10³⁷ and the reaction goes essentially to completion; a positive E°cell corresponds to negative ΔG° and K > 1, while E°cell = 0 at equilibrium of the standard state means K = 1
D) ΔG° = −212 J mol⁻¹; log K = 3.73
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ΔG° = −212.3 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ 37.3; K ≈ 2 × 10³⁷.
Concept: Electrical work done in one second is equal to electrical potential multiplied by total charge passed; if we want to obtain maximum work from a galvanic cell then charge has to be passed reversibly, and the reversible work done by a galvanic cell is equal to the decrease in its Gibbs energy: ΔrG = −nFEcell, where n is the number of moles of electrons and F is the Faraday constant; if the concentrations of all reacting species are unity, Ecell = E°cell and ΔrG° = −nFE°cell. If the circuit in a Daniell cell is closed, the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) takes place and as time passes the concentration of Zn²⁺ keeps on increasing while that of Cu²⁺ keeps on decreasing; at the same time the voltage of the cell keeps on decreasing, and after some time there is no change in the concentrations of Cu²⁺ and Zn²⁺ and the voltmeter gives zero reading — equilibrium has been attained. At equilibrium, Ecell = 0 and the Nernst equation gives E°cell = (2.303RT/nF) log Kc; at 298 K, E°cell = (0.059 V/n) log Kc. Since ΔrG° = −RT ln K = −nFE°, a positive E° means ΔG° is negative and K > 1, so the cell reaction is spontaneous.
Given: n = 2, E° = 1.10 V, F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: ΔG° = −nFE°; log K = nE°/0.059 at 298 K.
Step 1: ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 1.10 = −212 300 J mol⁻¹ = −212.3 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: log K = 2.20/0.059 = 37.3.
Step 3: K = 10^37.3 ≈ 2 × 10³⁷.
Why: The cell EMF measures the free-energy drop per coulomb, and a large positive EMF means an extremely large equilibrium constant.
Why not the others: (A) n omitted; E° > 0 means spontaneous. (B) Signs reversed. (D) Units off by 1000; log K mis-scaled.
Key point: ΔG° = −nFE°; log K = nE°/0.059; E° > 0 ⇔ ΔG° < 0 ⇔ K > 1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating average rate of a reaction from concentration–time data, expressing rates for different species using stoichiometric coefficients, and contrasting average with instantaneous rate
questions.question: For 2N₂O₅(g) → 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g), [N₂O₅] falls from 0.40 M to 0.32 M in 20 s. Find the average rate of reaction, the rate of formation of NO₂ and of O₂ over this interval. Which statement about instantaneous rate is correct?
options: A) Rate of reaction = −½ Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = ½(0.08/20) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; rate of formation of NO₂ = 8.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; of O₂ = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; the instantaneous rate at time t is the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at t, the limit of average rate as Δt → 0
B) Rate of reaction = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; NO₂ 4.0 × 10⁻³; O₂ 4.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹
C) Rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; NO₂ 2.0 × 10⁻³; O₂ 8.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; instantaneous rate is the average over the whole reaction
D) Rate = −4.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹ (rates are negative); NO₂ 1.6 × 10⁻²
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Rate 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; NO₂ 8.0 × 10⁻³; O₂ 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹; instantaneous rate = slope of tangent.
Concept: The speed of a reaction or the rate of a reaction can be defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product in unit time; it can be expressed in terms of the rate of decrease in concentration of any one of the reactants or the rate of increase in concentration of any one of the products. For R → P, average rate rav = −Δ[R]/Δt = +Δ[P]/Δt; the negative sign makes the rate positive because Δ[R] is negative. The average rate depends upon the change in concentration of reactants or products and the time taken for that change to occur, and it changes with time since the concentration decreases; hence it cannot be used to predict the rate at a particular moment; for that we determine the instantaneous rate, which is obtained when we consider the average rate at the smallest time interval, say dt (i.e., when Δt approaches zero): rinst = −d[R]/dt = d[P]/dt; it can be determined graphically by drawing a tangent at time t on either of the curves for concentration of R and P versus time and calculating its slope. When stoichiometric coefficients of reactants or products are not equal to one, the rate of disappearance of any reactant or rate of appearance of any product is divided by its stoichiometric coefficient: for aA + bB → cC + dD, rate = −(1/a)Δ[A]/Δt = −(1/b)Δ[B]/Δt = (1/c)Δ[C]/Δt = (1/d)Δ[D]/Δt.
Given: Δ[N₂O₅] = −0.08 M; Δt = 20 s.
Formula/Principle: Rate = −½ Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = ¼ Δ[NO₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt.
Step 1: −Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = 0.08/20 = 4.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹ ⇒ rate = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹.
Step 2: Δ[NO₂]/Δt = 4 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 8.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹.
Step 3: Δ[O₂]/Δt = 1 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M s⁻¹.
Why: Dividing each species' rate by its coefficient gives a single rate for the reaction.
Why not the others: (B) Coefficients ignored. (C) NO₂ and O₂ rates swapped; instantaneous rate is the tangent slope. (D) Rates are positive; NO₂ rate wrong.
Key point: Rate = −(1/a)d[A]/dt = (1/d)d[D]/dt; instantaneous rate = tangent slope.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Writing electronic configurations of 3d elements and their ions including the Cr and Cu exceptions, and explaining the most common and maximum oxidation states across the series
questions.question: Which statement about the 3d series is correct?
options: A) Cr is [Ar]3d⁴4s² and Cu is [Ar]3d⁹4s²; Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁴4s²
B) Electrons are removed from 3d before 4s when the ions form; zinc shows variable oxidation states
C) Sc shows +7 and Mn shows only +2

D) Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ because half-filled and completely filled d subshells are extra stable; on ionisation 4s electrons are removed first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵; the number of oxidation states rises to a maximum at manganese (+2 to +7, the highest equal to the sum of 3d and 4s electrons) and then falls, Sc showing only +3 and Zn only +2, while +2 is the common state for most of the later elements
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cr 3d⁵4s¹, Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹; 4s electrons lost first; oxidation states peak at Mn (+7).
Concept: In general the electronic configuration of the outer orbitals of these elements is (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ns¹⁻²; the (n−1) stands for the inner d orbitals which may have one to ten electrons, and the outermost ns orbital may have one or two electrons; however, this generalisation has several exceptions because of very little energy difference between (n−1)d and ns orbitals, and half and completely filled sets of orbitals are relatively more stable. A consequence of this factor is reflected in the electronic configurations of Cr and Cu in the 3d series: consider the case of Cr, for example, which has 3d⁵4s¹ instead of 3d⁴4s²; the energy gap between the two sets (3d and 4s) of orbitals is small enough to prevent electron entering the 3d orbitals; similarly in the case of Cu, the configuration is 3d¹⁰4s¹ and not 3d⁹4s². When transition metals form cations, the 4s electrons are lost first, since once the 3d orbitals are occupied they lie lower in energy than 4s. One of the notable features of transition elements is the great variety of oxidation states these may show in their compounds; the elements which give the greatest number of oxidation states occur in or near the middle of the series; manganese, for example, exhibits all the oxidation states from +2 to +7; the lesser number of oxidation states at the extreme ends stems from either too few electrons to lose or share (Sc, Ti) or too many d electrons (hence fewer orbitals available in which to share electrons with others) for higher valence (Cu, Zn); thus early in the series scandium(II) is virtually unknown and titanium(IV) is more stable than Ti(III) or Ti(II), and at the other end the only oxidation state of zinc is +2 (no d electrons are involved). The maximum oxidation states of reasonable stability correspond in value to the sum of the s and d electrons up to manganese (TiO₂, VO₂⁺, CrO₄²⁻, MnO₄⁻), followed by a rather abrupt decrease in stability of higher oxidation states.
Why: Half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable, and the number of available valence electrons decides the oxidation-state range.
Why not the others: (A) Wrong ground states for Cr and Cu; Fe²⁺ has lost its 4s electrons. (B) 4s electrons are lost first; Zn shows only +2. (C) Sc shows only +3; Mn shows +2 to +7.
Key point: Cr 3d⁵4s¹, Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹; ions lose 4s first; max oxidation states peak at Mn (+7).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Recognising ionisation, hydrate, linkage and coordination isomerism in coordination compounds and the experimental tests that distinguish them
questions.question: Which matching of isomer pairs with type of structural isomerism is correct?
options: A) [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ — linkage; [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ and [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O — coordination

B) [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ — ionisation isomers (the first gives a pale yellow precipitate with AgNO₃, the second a white precipitate with BaCl₂); [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) and [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (grey-green) — hydrate (solvate) isomers, distinguished by the number of Cl⁻ precipitated by AgNO₃; [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ and [Co(NH₃)₅(ONO)]Cl₂ — linkage isomers, the ambidentate NO₂⁻ binding through N or O; [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆] — coordination isomers, ligands interchanged between cationic and anionic complexes
C) All four pairs are geometrical isomers
D) [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ and [Co(NH₃)₅(ONO)]Cl₂ are ionisation isomers since they give different ions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ionisation, hydrate, linkage and coordination isomers correctly identified with tests.
Concept: Isomers are two or more compounds that have the same chemical formula but a different arrangement of atoms; structural isomers have different bonds. Linkage isomerism arises in a coordination compound containing an ambidentate ligand; a simple example is provided by complexes containing the thiocyanate ligand, NCS⁻, which may bind through the nitrogen to give M–NCS or through sulphur to give M–SCN; Jørgensen discovered such behaviour in the complex [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂, which is obtained as the red form, in which the nitrite ligand is bound through oxygen (–ONO), and as the yellow form, in which the nitrite ligand is bound through nitrogen (–NO₂). Coordination isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in a complex; an example is provided by [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆], in which the NH₃ ligands are bound to Co³⁺ and the CN⁻ ligands to Cr³⁺, while in its coordination isomer [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆] the NH₃ ligands are bound to Cr³⁺ and the CN⁻ ligands to Co³⁺. Ionisation isomerism arises when the counter ion in a complex salt is itself a potential ligand and can displace a ligand which can then become the counter ion; an example is provided by the ionisation isomers [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄. Solvate isomerism is a form of isomerism known as 'hydrate isomerism' in case water is involved as a solvent; this is similar to ionisation isomerism — solvate isomers differ by whether or not a solvent molecule is directly bonded to the metal ion or merely present as free solvent molecules in the crystal lattice; an example is provided by the aqua complex [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) and its solvate isomer [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (grey-green).
Why: Each type changes which group is inside the coordination sphere, or which donor atom binds, without changing the formula.
Why not the others: (A) Pairs mislabelled. (C) These differ in bonding (structural), not spatial arrangement. (D) They differ in the donor atom — linkage isomerism.
Key point: Ionisation: counter-ion ↔ ligand; hydrate: H₂O in/out of sphere; linkage: ambidentate donor; coordination: ligand swap between metals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking acidity of phenol and substituted phenols relative to alcohols and water using resonance stabilisation of phenoxide and inductive and resonance effects of substituents
questions.question: Arrange ethanol, water, phenol, o-nitrophenol, p-nitrophenol, p-cresol and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol in increasing order of acidity, and give the correct reason.
options: A) Phenol < ethanol < water < p-cresol < o-nitrophenol < p-nitrophenol < picric acid

B) Ethanol < water < p-cresol < phenol < o-nitrophenol < p-nitrophenol < 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid); phenoxide is stabilised by delocalising the negative charge over the ring, alkoxide is not and the alkyl group's +I effect destabilises it; electron-withdrawing –NO₂ at ortho and para positions further delocalises the charge (–R and –I effects), so acidity rises with more nitro groups, while electron-releasing –CH₃ destabilises phenoxide and lowers acidity; o-nitrophenol is slightly less acidic than p-nitrophenol because intramolecular hydrogen bonding holds its proton
C) All phenols have the same acidity because they share the –OH group
D) p-Cresol is more acidic than p-nitrophenol because –CH₃ is electron releasing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ethanol < water < p-cresol < phenol < o-nitrophenol < p-nitrophenol < picric acid.
Concept: The reaction of phenol with aqueous sodium hydroxide indicates that phenols are stronger acids than alcohols and water. The hydroxyl group in phenol is directly attached to the sp² hybridised carbon of the benzene ring, which acts as an electron-withdrawing group; due to this, the charge distribution in the phenol molecule causes the oxygen of the –OH group to be positive. The reaction of phenol with aqueous sodium hydroxide indicates that phenols are stronger acids; in the phenoxide ion, the negative charge is delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance, which makes phenoxide more stable than phenol (whose resonance structures involve charge separation), whereas in the alkoxide ion the negative charge is localised on oxygen. In substituted phenols, the presence of electron-withdrawing groups such as the nitro group enhances the acidic strength of phenol; this effect is more pronounced when such a group is present at ortho and para positions, because of the effective delocalisation of the negative charge in phenoxide ion. On the other hand, electron-releasing groups such as alkyl groups, in general, do not favour the formation of phenoxide ion, resulting in a decrease in acid strength; cresols, for example, are less acidic than phenol. The pKa values are approximately: ethanol 15.9, water 15.7, p-cresol 10.2, phenol 10.0, o-nitrophenol 7.2, p-nitrophenol 7.1, and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol 0.5.
Why: The more the conjugate base's negative charge is spread out, the more readily the proton is released.
Why not the others: (A) Phenol is more acidic than ethanol and water. (C) Substituents change acidity strongly. (D) –CH₃ lowers acidity; –NO₂ raises it.
Key point: Phenoxide resonance makes phenol acidic; –NO₂ (o/p) increases, –CH₃ decreases acidity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting products of electrophilic substitution of phenol (bromination, nitration) and of Kolbe's and Reimer–Tiemann reactions, and the directing effect of –OH
questions.question: Which set of products from phenol is correct?
options: A) Phenol + bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, while Br₂ in CS₂ at low temperature gives mainly mono-bromophenols (o- and p-); dilute HNO₃ at 298 K gives o- and p-nitrophenol (separable by steam distillation, the ortho isomer being steam volatile due to intramolecular H-bonding), while concentrated HNO₃ gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol; sodium phenoxide + CO₂ under pressure followed by acid gives salicylic acid (Kolbe's reaction); phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH followed by acid gives salicylaldehyde (Reimer–Tiemann reaction); –OH activates the ring and is ortho/para directing
B) Phenol + bromine water gives only m-bromophenol; –OH is meta directing
C) Kolbe's reaction gives benzaldehyde; Reimer–Tiemann gives benzoic acid
D) Dilute HNO₃ gives only picric acid; p-nitrophenol is steam volatile
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bromination, nitration, Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann products correctly given; –OH is o/p directing and activating.
Concept: In phenols, the reactions that take place on the aromatic ring are electrophilic substitution reactions; the –OH group attached to the benzene ring activates it towards electrophilic substitution, and it also directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions in the ring as these positions become electron rich due to the resonance effect caused by the –OH group. With dilute nitric acid at low temperature (298 K), phenol yields a mixture of ortho and para nitrophenols; the ortho and para isomers can be separated by steam distillation — o-nitrophenol is steam volatile due to intramolecular hydrogen bonding while p-nitrophenol is less volatile due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which causes the association of molecules. With concentrated nitric acid, phenol is converted to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, commonly known as picric acid; the yield of the reaction product is poor. On treating phenol with bromine, different reaction products are formed under different experimental conditions: when the reaction is carried out in solvents of low polarity such as CHCl₃ or CS₂ and at low temperature, monobromophenols are formed; the usual halogenation of benzene takes place in the presence of a Lewis acid, such as FeBr₃, which polarises the halogen molecule, but in the case of phenol the polarisation of the bromine molecule takes place even in the absence of a Lewis acid due to the highly activating effect of the –OH group attached to the benzene ring. When phenol is treated with bromine water, 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed as a white precipitate. Kolbe's reaction: the phenoxide ion generated by treating phenol with sodium hydroxide is even more reactive than phenol towards electrophilic aromatic substitution; hence it undergoes electrophilic substitution with carbon dioxide, a weak electrophile, and ortho-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid) is formed as the main product. Reimer–Tiemann reaction: on treating phenol with chloroform in the presence of sodium hydroxide, a –CHO group is introduced at the ortho position of the benzene ring; the intermediate substituted benzal chloride is hydrolysed in the presence of alkali to produce salicylaldehyde.
Why: The –OH group strongly donates electron density by resonance to ortho and para positions, making these sites very reactive.
Why not the others: (B) Bromine water gives the tribromo product; –OH is o/p directing. (C) Kolbe gives salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann gives salicylaldehyde. (D) Dilute HNO₃ gives mononitrophenols; the ortho isomer is steam volatile.
Key point: Bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol; Kolbe → salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann → salicylaldehyde.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing aldehydes and ketones by Tollens', Fehling's and iodoform tests, and identifying reduction products from Clemmensen, Wolff–Kishner and NaBH4
questions.question: Three unlabelled liquids are ethanal, propanone and benzaldehyde. Which set of test results is correct?
options: A) All three give silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and red precipitate with Fehling's
B) Propanone gives silver mirror; ethanal does not react with Fehling's; benzaldehyde gives iodoform
C) Only propanone reduces Fehling's solution

D) Ethanal: Tollens' positive (silver mirror), Fehling's positive (red-brown Cu₂O), iodoform positive (has CH₃CO–); propanone: Tollens' and Fehling's negative, iodoform positive (yellow CHI₃); benzaldehyde: Tollens' positive but Fehling's negative (aromatic aldehydes do not respond), iodoform negative; Clemmensen (Zn–Hg/HCl) or Wolff–Kishner (NH₂NH₂ then KOH in ethylene glycol) reduces C=O to CH₂, and NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes to primary and ketones to secondary alcohols
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ethanal: Tollens' +, Fehling's +, iodoform +; propanone: iodoform only; benzaldehyde: Tollens' only.
Concept: Aldehydes differ from ketones in their oxidation reactions; aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids on treatment with common oxidising agents like nitric acid, potassium permanganate, potassium dichromate, etc.; even mild oxidising agents, mainly Tollens' reagent and Fehling's reagent, also oxidise aldehydes. Ketones are generally oxidised under vigorous conditions, i.e., strong oxidising agents and at elevated temperatures. Tollens' test: on warming an aldehyde with freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution (Tollens' reagent), a bright silver mirror is produced due to the formation of silver metal; the aldehydes are oxidised to the corresponding carboxylate anion. Fehling's test: Fehling reagent comprises two solutions, Fehling solution A (aqueous copper sulphate) and Fehling solution B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate); these two solutions are mixed in equal amounts before the test; on heating an aldehyde with Fehling's reagent, a reddish-brown precipitate is obtained; aldehydes are oxidised to the corresponding carboxylate anion, and aromatic aldehydes do not respond to this test. Oxidation of methyl ketones by the haloform reaction: aldehydes and ketones having at least one methyl group linked to the carbonyl carbon atom (methyl ketones) are oxidised by sodium hypohalite to sodium salts of corresponding carboxylic acids having one carbon atom less than that of the carbonyl compound; the methyl group is converted to haloform, and the iodoform reaction with sodium hypoiodite is also used for detection of the CH₃CO group or CH₃CH(OH) group which produces CH₃CO group on oxidation. Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to primary and secondary alcohols respectively by sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) or lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) as well as by catalytic hydrogenation. The carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones is reduced to a CH₂ group on treatment with zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid (Clemmensen reduction) or with hydrazine followed by heating with sodium or potassium hydroxide in a high boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol (Wolff–Kishner reduction).
Why: Aldehydes are easily oxidised; Fehling's needs an aliphatic aldehyde; the iodoform test needs a CH₃CO– group.
Why not the others: (A) Propanone fails Tollens' and Fehling's; benzaldehyde fails Fehling's. (B) Propanone fails Tollens'; ethanal reduces Fehling's; benzaldehyde lacks CH₃CO–. (C) Propanone does not reduce Fehling's.
Key point: Tollens' all aldehydes; Fehling's aliphatic aldehydes only; iodoform needs CH₃CO–.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking acid strength of substituted carboxylic acids using inductive effects, number and position of electron-withdrawing groups, and comparing benzoic acids with aliphatic acids
questions.question: Which order of acid strength is correct?
options: A) 4-chlorobutanoic acid > 3-chlorobutanoic acid > 2-chlorobutanoic acid
B) CH₃COOH > HCOOH > ClCH₂COOH > CF₃COOH

C) CF₃COOH > CCl₃COOH > CHCl₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > HCOOH > CH₃COOH; 2-chlorobutanoic acid > 3-chlorobutanoic acid > 4-chlorobutanoic acid; p-nitrobenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-methoxybenzoic acid; electron-withdrawing groups stabilise the carboxylate anion by dispersing its negative charge (–I effect, strongest when close to –COOH and increasing with number and electronegativity of groups), while electron-donating groups destabilise it and decrease acidity
D) p-Methoxybenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-nitrobenzoic acid
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) All three orders correctly ranked by inductive and resonance effects.
Concept: Carboxylic acids are weaker than mineral acids but stronger than alcohols and many simple phenols; the higher acidity of carboxylic acids compared with phenols can be attributed to the conjugate base, carboxylate ion, being stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures in which the negative charge is at the more electronegative oxygen atom. Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) increase the acidity of carboxylic acids by stabilising the conjugate base through delocalisation of the negative charge by inductive and/or resonance effects; conversely, electron-donating groups decrease the acidity by destabilising the conjugate base. The effect of the following groups in increasing acidity order is Ph < I < Br < Cl < F < CN < NO₂ < CF₃; thus, the following acids are arranged in order of increasing acidity (based on pKa values): CF₃COOH > CCl₃COOH > CCl₂HCOOH > NO₂CH₂COOH > NC–CH₂COOH > FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > BrCH₂COOH > HCOOH > ClCH₂CH₂COOH > C₆H₅COOH > C₆H₅CH₂COOH > CH₃COOH > CH₃CH₂COOH. Direct attachment of groups such as phenyl or vinyl to the carboxylic acid increases its acidity, contrary to the decrease expected due to the resonance effect, because of the greater electronegativity of the sp² hybridised carbon to which the carboxyl carbon is attached. The inductive effect decreases rapidly with distance, so a chlorine at the α-position increases acidity more than one at β or γ. The presence of an electron-withdrawing group on the phenyl of aromatic carboxylic acid increases their acidity while electron-donating groups decrease their acidity.
Why: Anything that spreads out the negative charge of the carboxylate ion favours ionisation.
Why not the others: (A) The –I effect weakens with distance. (B) Order reversed. (D) –NO₂ increases and –OCH₃ decreases acidity.
Key point: More, stronger and closer EWGs ⇒ stronger acid; EDGs weaken.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding n from a given value of a combination, counting committees with an at-least condition, and finding the number of sides of a polygon from its number of diagonals
questions.question: Find \(n\) if \(^nC_2=45\). In how many ways can a committee of 5 be chosen from 6 men and 4 women so that it has at least 3 women? How many sides has a polygon with 44 diagonals?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(n=10;\ 66;\ 11\text{ sides}\)
Concept: \(\text{selection without order uses }^nC_r=\dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!};\ \text{an at-least condition is split into disjoint cases and added}\)
Given: \(^nC_2=45;\ 6\text{ men},\ 4\text{ women},\ 5\text{ members};\ 44\text{ diagonals}\)
Formula/Principle: \(^nC_2=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2};\ \text{diagonals}=\,^nC_2-n=\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}\)
Step 1: \(n(n-1)=90\Rightarrow n=10\)
Step 2: \(\text{3 women: }^4C_3\cdot\,^6C_2=4\times15=60;\ \text{4 women: }^4C_4\cdot\,^6C_1=6;\ \text{total }66\)
Step 3: \(n(n-3)=88\Rightarrow n^2-3n-88=0\Rightarrow(n-11)(n+8)=0\Rightarrow n=11\)
Worked derivation: \[\binom43\binom62+\binom44\binom61=4\cdot15+1\cdot6=66\]
Check: \[\frac{11\times8}{2}=44\ \checkmark;\quad\frac{10\times9}{2}=45\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each case of the at-least condition counts different committees, so the cases add}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(^9C_2=36;\ \text{the 4-women case is missed}\); (B) \(126=\,^9C_4\text{ is unrelated}\); (D) \(n\text{ confused with the value}\).
Key point: \(\text{at least}\Rightarrow\text{sum of exact cases};\ \text{diagonals}=n(n-3)/2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the middle term of a binomial expansion with an even index and the term independent of x by setting the power of x to zero
questions.question: Find the middle term of \(\left(2x-\dfrac1x\right)^{10}\), the number of terms in it, and the term independent of \(x\) in \(\left(x^2+\dfrac1x\right)^9\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(T_6=-8064;\ 11\text{ terms};\ T_7=84\)
Concept: \((a+b)^n\text{ has }n+1\text{ terms};\ \text{for even }n\text{ the middle term is }T_{n/2+1};\ \text{the general term is }T_{r+1}=\,^nC_r\,a^{n-r}b^r\)
Given: \(n=10,\ a=2x,\ b=-\tfrac1x;\ n=9,\ a=x^2,\ b=\tfrac1x\)
Formula/Principle: \(T_{r+1}=\,^nC_r\,a^{n-r}b^r\)
Step 1: \(\text{11 terms; middle }T_6:\ ^{10}C_5(2x)^5\left(-\tfrac1x\right)^5=252\times32\times(-1)=-8064\)
Step 2: \(T_{r+1}=\,^9C_r\,x^{18-2r}x^{-r}=\,^9C_r\,x^{18-3r}\)
Step 3: \(18-3r=0\Rightarrow r=6\Rightarrow\,^9C_6=84\)
Worked derivation: \[T_6=\binom{10}{5}(2x)^5\left(-\frac1x\right)^5=252\cdot32x^5\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{x^5}\right)=-8064\]
Check: \[\binom96=\binom93=\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7}{6}=84\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the powers of }x\text{ cancel exactly in both the middle term and the }r=6\text{ term}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{sign lost; }n+1\text{ terms}\); (C) \(\text{the factor }2^5\text{ is missed}\); (D) \(x\text{ cancels; 11 terms}\).
Key point: \(T_{r+1}=\,^nC_ra^{n-r}b^r;\ \text{set the power of }x\text{ to }0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Reading focus, directrix and latus rectum of a parabola, finding points at a given focal distance, and finding a parabola with vertical axis through a given point
questions.question: For \(y^2=12x\) find the focus, directrix and length of latus rectum, and the points on it whose distance from the focus is 8. Find also the parabola with vertex at the origin, axis along the \(y\)-axis, passing through \((2,3)\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\text{focus }(3,0),\ x=-3,\ \text{LR}=12;\ (5,\pm2\sqrt{15});\ x^2=\tfrac43y\)
Concept: \(\text{a parabola is the locus of points equidistant from the focus and the directrix, so the focal distance of }(x,y)\text{ on }y^2=4ax\text{ is }x+a\)
Given: \(y^2=12x\Rightarrow4a=12,\ a=3;\ \text{point }(2,3)\)
Formula/Principle: \(y^2=4ax:\ S(a,0),\ x=-a,\ \text{LR}=4a,\ SP=x+a;\ x^2=4by\)
Step 1: \(S=(3,0),\ \text{directrix }x=-3,\ \text{LR}=12\)
Step 2: \(x+3=8\Rightarrow x=5,\ y^2=60\Rightarrow y=\pm2\sqrt{15}\)
Step 3: \(x^2=4by:\ 4=12b\Rightarrow b=\tfrac13\Rightarrow x^2=\tfrac43y\)
Worked derivation: \[SP=\sqrt{(5-3)^2+60}=\sqrt{64}=8\]
Check: \[(2)^2=\frac43(3)=4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the focal distance equals the distance to the directrix, which is }x+a\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{axis wrong}\); (B) \(\text{directrix is }x=-3,\ \text{LR}=12\); (C) \(a=3,\ \text{not }12\).
Key point: \(y^2=4ax:\ SP=x+a,\ \text{LR}=4a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding derivatives of x squared and 1/x from first principles, and interpreting a derivative as the rate of change of the area of a circle with radius
questions.question: Using first principles, find the derivatives of \(x^2\) and \(\dfrac1x\). At what rate does the area of a circle change with respect to its radius when \(r=5\text{ cm}\)?
options: A) \(2x;\ \dfrac1{x^2};\ 25\pi\text{ cm}^2\text{ per cm}\)
B) \(2x;\ -\dfrac1{x^2};\ 10\pi\text{ cm}^2\text{ per cm}\)
C) \(x;\ -\dfrac1x;\ 5\pi\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2x;\ -\dfrac1{x^2};\ 10\pi\text{ cm}^2\text{ per cm}\)
Concept: \(f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\text{ is the slope of the tangent and the instantaneous rate of change}\)
Given: \(f(x)=x^2,\ g(x)=\tfrac1x;\ A=\pi r^2,\ r=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h}=2x+h\to2x\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{\frac1{x+h}-\frac1x}{h}=\dfrac{-1}{x(x+h)}\to-\dfrac1{x^2}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{dA}{dr}=2\pi r=10\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{1}{h}\left(\frac{1}{x+h}-\frac1x\right)=\frac{x-(x+h)}{hx(x+h)}=\frac{-1}{x(x+h)}\]
Check: \[\frac{dA}{dr}=2\pi r=\text{circumference, the thin ring added per unit increase of }r\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the limit removes the }h\text{ terms, leaving the exact slope}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign lost; rate is }2\pi r\); (C) \(\text{limits wrong}\); (D) \(h\text{ must go to }0\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}x^2=2x;\ \dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac1x=-\dfrac1{x^2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding an unknown observation from a given mean, then the range and mean deviation about the mean, and how they change when the data are shifted or scaled
questions.question: The observations \(2,4,6,8,x\) have mean 6. Find \(x\), the range, and the mean deviation about the mean. What happens to the mean deviation if each observation is increased by 5, and if each is multiplied by 3?
options: A) \(x=10;\ 8;\ 2.4;\ \text{rises by 5};\ \text{unchanged}\)
B) \(x=10;\ 8;\ 2.4;\ \text{unchanged};\ \text{becomes }7.2\)
C) \(x=8;\ 6;\ 2;\ \text{unchanged};\ 6\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(x=10;\ \text{range }8;\ \text{MD}=2.4;\ \text{unchanged by shift};\ 7.2\text{ after scaling}\)
Concept: \(\text{mean deviation about the mean measures average distance from the mean; a shift moves every value and the mean equally, while scaling multiplies every distance}\)
Given: \(\bar x=6,\ n=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{MD}(\bar x)=\dfrac{\sum|x_i-\bar x|}{n};\ \text{range}=\max-\min\)
Step 1: \(2+4+6+8+x=30\Rightarrow x=10;\ \text{range}=10-2=8\)
Step 2: \(|x_i-6|=4,2,0,2,4\Rightarrow\sum=12\Rightarrow\text{MD}=2.4\)
Step 3: \(x_i+5\Rightarrow\text{MD}=2.4;\ 3x_i\Rightarrow\text{MD}=3\times2.4=7.2\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{MD}(ax_i+b)=\frac{\sum|ax_i+b-(a\bar x+b)|}{n}=|a|\,\text{MD}(x_i)\]
Check: \[\text{scaled data }6,12,18,24,30:\ \text{mean }18,\ \text{deviations }12,6,0,6,12,\ \tfrac{36}{5}=7.2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{dispersion measures ignore shifts but scale with the data}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{shift does not change MD; scaling does}\); (C) \(x\text{ wrong}\); (D) \(\text{range and MD wrong}\).
Key point: \(\text{MD}(ax+b)=|a|\,\text{MD}(x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the multiplication theorem for drawing without replacement and the product rule for independent events to find union and neither probabilities
questions.question: A bag has 5 red and 3 black balls. Two are drawn one after another without replacement; find the probability both are red. Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent with \(P(A)=0.3,\ P(B)=0.4\); find \(P(A\cup B)\) and the probability that neither occurs.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\tfrac{5}{14};\ 0.58;\ 0.42\)
Concept: \(P(E\cap F)=P(E)P(F\mid E);\ \text{for independent events }P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\text{ and complements are also independent}\)
Given: \(5R,3B;\ P(A)=0.3,\ P(B)=0.4\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(E\cap F)=P(E)P(F\mid E);\ P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)\)
Step 1: \(P(RR)=\tfrac58\cdot\tfrac47=\tfrac{20}{56}=\tfrac5{14}\)
Step 2: \(P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.4-0.12=0.58\)
Step 3: \(P(A'\cap B')=0.7\times0.6=0.42\)
Worked derivation: \[P(A'\cap B')=1-P(A\cup B)=1-0.58=0.42=P(A')P(B')\]
Check: \[\frac{\binom52}{\binom82}=\frac{10}{28}=\frac5{14}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{without replacement the second draw depends on the first, so the conditional probability is used}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{assumes replacement; union adds without subtracting}\); (B) \(\text{gives }P(A\cap B)\text{ as the union}\); (C) \(\text{wrong second factor; neither is not }0.12\).
Key point: \(P(E\cap F)=P(E)P(F|E);\ \text{independent}\Rightarrow\text{multiply}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the theorem of total probability to a two-bag experiment and finding an unknown number of balls that makes the overall probability equal to a given value
questions.question: A die is thrown; if it shows 1 or 2 a ball is drawn from bag I (3 red, 2 white), otherwise from bag II (2 red, 4 white). Find \(P(\text{red})\). In another experiment a fair coin chooses between bag P (2 red, 3 white) and bag Q (\(k\) red, \(5-k\) white); find \(k\) if \(P(\text{red})=\tfrac12\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\tfrac{19}{45};\ k=3\)
Concept: \(\text{if }E_1,E_2\text{ partition the sample space, }P(A)=P(E_1)P(A\mid E_1)+P(E_2)P(A\mid E_2)\)
Given: \(P(E_1)=\tfrac13,\ P(E_2)=\tfrac23;\ \text{coin }\tfrac12,\tfrac12\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A)=\sum P(E_i)P(A\mid E_i)\)
Step 1: \(P(R)=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac35+\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac26=\tfrac15+\tfrac29\)
Step 2: \(=\tfrac{9+10}{45}=\tfrac{19}{45}\)
Step 3: \(\tfrac12\left(\tfrac25+\tfrac k5\right)=\tfrac12\Rightarrow2+k=5\Rightarrow k=3\)
Worked derivation: \[P(R)=\frac{2+k}{10}=\frac12\Rightarrow k=3\]
Check: \[k=3:\ \tfrac12\left(\tfrac25+\tfrac35\right)=\tfrac12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the overall probability is a weighted average of the conditional probabilities}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{conditional probabilities added without weights}\); (C) \(\text{weights ignored}\); (D) \(k=4\text{ gives }\tfrac35\).
Key point: \(P(A)=\sum P(E_i)P(A|E_i)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving simultaneous matrix equations for two unknown matrices, finding unknown entries from a matrix equation, and the reversal law for the transpose of a product
questions.question: Find \(X\) and \(Y\) if \(X+Y=\begin{bmatrix}5&2\\0&9\end{bmatrix}\) and \(X-Y=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}\). Find \(x,y\) if \(2\begin{bmatrix}x&5\\7&y-3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3&-4\\1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&6\\15&14\end{bmatrix}\). Which transpose rule is correct?
options: A) \(X=\begin{bmatrix}8&8\\0&8\end{bmatrix};\ x=4,\ y=6;\ (AB)^T=A^TB^T\)
B) \(X=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&5\end{bmatrix},\ Y=\begin{bmatrix}4&4\\0&4\end{bmatrix};\ x=2,\ y=8;\ (AB)^T=B^TA^T\)
C) \(X=\begin{bmatrix}4&4\\0&4\end{bmatrix},\ Y=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&5\end{bmatrix};\ x=2,\ y=9;\ (AB)^T=B^TA^T\)
D) \(X=\begin{bmatrix}4&4\\0&4\end{bmatrix},\ Y=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&5\end{bmatrix};\ x=5,\ y=9;\ (AB)^T=AB\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(X=\begin{bmatrix}4&4\\0&4\end{bmatrix},\ Y=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&5\end{bmatrix};\ x=2,\ y=9;\ (AB)^T=B^TA^T\)
Concept: \(\text{matrices of the same order add entrywise, so matrix equations can be solved like ordinary simultaneous equations; equal matrices have equal corresponding entries}\)
Given: \(X+Y,\ X-Y\text{ known};\ \text{entrywise equation}\)
Formula/Principle: \(X=\tfrac12[(X+Y)+(X-Y)],\ Y=\tfrac12[(X+Y)-(X-Y)];\ (AB)^T=B^TA^T\)
Step 1: \(2X=\begin{bmatrix}8&8\\0&8\end{bmatrix}\Rightarrow X=\begin{bmatrix}4&4\\0&4\end{bmatrix};\ 2Y=\begin{bmatrix}2&-4\\0&10\end{bmatrix}\Rightarrow Y=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&5\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(2x+3=7\Rightarrow x=2\)
Step 3: \(2(y-3)+2=14\Rightarrow y=9\)
Worked derivation: \[\begin{bmatrix}2x+3&10-4\\14+1&2y-6+2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&6\\15&14\end{bmatrix}\]
Check: \[X+Y=\begin{bmatrix}5&2\\0&9\end{bmatrix},\ X-Y=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{adding and subtracting the two equations isolates }X\text{ and }Y\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgot to halve; order reversed in the transpose rule}\); (B) \(X\text{ and }Y\text{ swapped; }y=9\); (D) \(x=2;\ (AB)^T\ne AB\text{ in general}\).
Key point: \((AB)^T=B^TA^T\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Expressing a square matrix as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix, and special properties of skew-symmetric matrices such as zero diagonal and zero determinant for odd order
questions.question: Express \(A=\begin{bmatrix}3&5\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}\) as \(P+Q\) with \(P\) symmetric and \(Q\) skew-symmetric. Which further statement is correct?
options: A) \(P=\begin{bmatrix}3&3\\3&-1\end{bmatrix},\ Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&2\\-2&0\end{bmatrix};\ \text{every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix is 0, a matrix both symmetric and skew-symmetric is the zero matrix, and a skew-symmetric matrix of odd order has determinant 0}\)
B) \(P=\begin{bmatrix}3&5\\5&-1\end{bmatrix},\ Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&-4\\4&0\end{bmatrix};\ \text{skew-symmetric matrices have diagonal entries 1}\)
C) \(P=\begin{bmatrix}6&6\\6&-2\end{bmatrix},\ Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&4\\-4&0\end{bmatrix};\ \text{odd-order skew-symmetric matrices are invertible}\)
D) \(P=\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix},\ Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&3\\-3&0\end{bmatrix};\ \text{the representation is not unique}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(P=\begin{bmatrix}3&3\\3&-1\end{bmatrix},\ Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&2\\-2&0\end{bmatrix}\); special properties correct.
Concept: \(\text{every square matrix is uniquely }A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T),\ \text{the first symmetric and the second skew-symmetric}\)
Given: \(A^T=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\5&-1\end{bmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=\tfrac12(A+A^T),\ Q=\tfrac12(A-A^T);\ Q^T=-Q\Rightarrow q_{ii}=0\)
Step 1: \(A+A^T=\begin{bmatrix}6&6\\6&-2\end{bmatrix}\Rightarrow P=\begin{bmatrix}3&3\\3&-1\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(A-A^T=\begin{bmatrix}0&4\\-4&0\end{bmatrix}\Rightarrow Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&2\\-2&0\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 3: \(\text{odd }n:\ \det Q=\det(Q^T)=\det(-Q)=(-1)^n\det Q=-\det Q\Rightarrow\det Q=0\)
Worked derivation: \[P+Q=\begin{bmatrix}3+0&3+2\\3-2&-1+0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&5\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}=A\]
Check: \[P^T=P,\ \ Q^T=\begin{bmatrix}0&-2\\2&0\end{bmatrix}=-Q\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{averaging }A\text{ with its transpose keeps the symmetric part; the difference keeps the skew part}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(P+Q\ne A\text{ and diagonal of }Q\text{ is }0\); (C) \(\text{forgot the factor }\tfrac12;\ \det=0\text{ for odd order}\); (D) \(\text{sum does not give }A;\ \text{the split is unique}\).
Key point: \(A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
