questions.sub_topic: Differentiating an implicit curve to find a slope and counting points with horizontal tangents, and counting points where an inverse-trigonometric composite fails to be differentiable
questions.question: For \(x^2+xy+y^2=7\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \((1,2)\) and the number of points on the curve where the tangent is horizontal. At how many points is \(y=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)\) not differentiable?
options: D) \(-\tfrac45;\ 2;\ 2\ (x=\pm1),\ \text{since }y'=\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\text{ for }|x|<1\text{ and }-\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\text{ for }|x|>1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(-\tfrac45;\ 2\text{ points};\ \text{not differentiable at }x=\pm1\)
Concept: \(\text{implicit differentiation treats }y\text{ as a function of }x;\ \text{with }x=\tan\theta,\ \sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\text{ equals }2\tan^{-1}x\text{ only for }|x|\le1\)
Given: \(x^2+xy+y^2=7;\ y=\sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(2x+y+xy'+2yy'=0\Rightarrow y'=-\dfrac{2x+y}{x+2y}\)
Step 1: \(\text{at }(1,2):\ y'=-\dfrac{4}{5}\)
Step 2: \(y'=0\Rightarrow y=-2x\Rightarrow x^2-2x^2+4x^2=7\Rightarrow x=\pm\sqrt{7/3}\Rightarrow2\text{ points}\)
Step 3: \(\text{left and right derivatives at }x=1:\ +1\text{ and }-1\Rightarrow\text{corner};\ \text{same at }x=-1\)
Worked derivation: \[y=\begin{cases}2\tan^{-1}x,&|x|\le1\\ \pi-2\tan^{-1}x,&x>1\\ -\pi-2\tan^{-1}x,&x<-1\end{cases}\]
Check: \[x=\sqrt{7/3},\ y=-2\sqrt{7/3}:\ \tfrac73-\tfrac{14}{3}+\tfrac{28}{3}=7\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the branch of }\sin^{-1}\text{ switches at }|x|=1,\ \text{where the curve has a corner}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only two horizontal tangents; corners exist}\); (B) \(\text{sign and count wrong}\); (C) \(\text{slope inverted}\).
Key point: \(y'=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_y};\ \sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\text{ has corners at }x=\pm1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using logarithmic differentiation to find the slope of a product–quotient curve at a point and locating the horizontal tangent of x to the power 1/x
questions.question: For \(y=\dfrac{(x+1)^2(x+2)^3}{(x+3)^4}\), find the slope of the curve at \(x=0\). Where does \(y=x^{1/x}\ (x>0)\) have a horizontal tangent, and what is its value there?
options: B) \(\tfrac{52}{243};\ x=e,\ y=e^{1/e}\ (\text{maximum})\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\text{slope }\tfrac{52}{243};\ \text{horizontal tangent at }x=e,\ y=e^{1/e}\)
Concept: \(\text{taking logarithms turns products, quotients and variable powers into sums, which are easy to differentiate}\)
Given: \(y(0)=\dfrac{1\cdot8}{81}=\dfrac8{81}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{y'}{y}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln y\)
Step 1: \(\ln y=2\ln(x+1)+3\ln(x+2)-4\ln(x+3)\Rightarrow\dfrac{y'}{y}=\dfrac2{x+1}+\dfrac3{x+2}-\dfrac4{x+3}\)
Step 2: \(\text{at }0:\ 2+\tfrac32-\tfrac43=\tfrac{13}{6}\Rightarrow y'=\tfrac8{81}\cdot\tfrac{13}6=\tfrac{52}{243}\)
Step 3: \(\ln y=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\Rightarrow\dfrac{y'}{y}=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}=0\Rightarrow x=e\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{8}{81}\cdot\frac{13}{6}=\frac{104}{486}=\frac{52}{243}\]
Check: \[\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}>0\text{ for }x<e,\ <0\text{ for }x>e\Rightarrow\text{maximum }e^{1/e}\approx1.44\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a horizontal tangent occurs where the derivative of }\ln y\text{ vanishes, since }y>0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac{13}{6}\text{ is }y'/y,\ \text{not }y'\); (C) \(8/81\text{ is }y(0)\); (D) \(\text{the critical point is }x=e\).
Key point: \(y'=y\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\ln y\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding absolute maximum and minimum of a cubic on a closed interval by comparing values at critical points and end points
questions.question: Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of \(f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+1\) on \([1,5]\).
options: A) \(\max29\text{ at }x=2;\ \min28\text{ at }x=3\)
B) \(\max56\text{ at }x=5;\ \min28\text{ at }x=3\)
C) \(\max56\text{ at }x=5;\ \min24\text{ at }x=1\)
D) \(\max29\text{ at }x=2;\ \min24\text{ at }x=1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\text{absolute max }56\text{ at }x=5;\ \text{absolute min }24\text{ at }x=1\)
Concept: \(\text{a continuous function on a closed interval attains its absolute extrema at critical points or end points}\)
Given: \([1,5]\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(x)=6x^2-30x+36=6(x-2)(x-3)\)
Step 1: \(\text{critical points }x=2,3\)
Step 2: \(f(1)=24,\ f(2)=29,\ f(3)=28,\ f(5)=56\)
Step 3: \(\max=56\ (x=5),\ \min=24\ (x=1)\)
Worked derivation: \[f(5)=250-375+180+1=56;\quad f(1)=2-15+36+1=24\]
Check: \[f(2)=16-60+72+1=29,\ f(3)=54-135+108+1=28\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{local extrema at }2\text{ and }3\text{ are beaten by the end-point values}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{local values, not absolute}\); (B) \(f(1)=24<28\); (D) \(f(5)=56>29\).
Key point: \(\text{compare }f\text{ at critical points and end points}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Integrating x e^x and inverse tangent by parts, and studying the increasing–decreasing behaviour and minimum of an accumulation function defined by an integral
questions.question: Find \(\displaystyle\int xe^x\,dx\) and \(\displaystyle\int\tan^{-1}x\,dx\). For \(F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x te^t\,dt\), find \(F(x)\), its minimum value and where it occurs.
options: A) \(x e^x;\ \dfrac1{1+x^2};\ \min\text{ at }x=1\)
B) \((x+1)e^x;\ x\tan^{-1}x+\tfrac12\ln(1+x^2);\ \max0\text{ at }x=0\)
C) \((x-1)e^x;\ x\tan^{-1}x;\ \text{no minimum}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \((x-1)e^x+C;\ x\tan^{-1}x-\tfrac12\ln(1+x^2)+C;\ F_{\min}=0\text{ at }x=0\)
Concept: \(\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du;\ \text{choose }u\text{ by ILATE so that }du\text{ is simpler}\)
Given: \(F'(x)=xe^x\)
Formula/Principle: \(\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du\)
Step 1: \(u=x,\ dv=e^xdx:\ xe^x-\int e^xdx=(x-1)e^x+C\)
Step 2: \(u=\tan^{-1}x,\ dv=dx:\ x\tan^{-1}x-\int\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}dx=x\tan^{-1}x-\tfrac12\ln(1+x^2)+C\)
Step 3: \(F(x)=[(t-1)e^t]_0^x=(x-1)e^x+1;\ F'(x)=xe^x<0\ (x<0),\ >0\ (x>0)\Rightarrow\min F(0)=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[(x-1)e^x\right]=e^x+(x-1)e^x=xe^x\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[x\tan^{-1}x-\tfrac12\ln(1+x^2)\right]=\tan^{-1}x+\frac{x}{1+x^2}-\frac{x}{1+x^2}=\tan^{-1}x\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the sign of the integrand decides where the accumulation function decreases or increases}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{derivatives given instead of integrals}\); (B) \(\text{signs wrong; }x=0\text{ is a minimum}\); (C) \(\text{missing the log term; }F\text{ has a minimum}\).
Key point: \(\int xe^x=(x-1)e^x;\ F'(x)=f(x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the area of the part of an ellipse lying between two vertical lines by trigonometric substitution, and the area of a circular sector cut off by a line through the origin
questions.question: Find the area of the part of the region \(\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}\le1\) lying between the lines \(x=-2\) and \(x=2\). Find also the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the \(x\)-axis, the line \(y=\sqrt3\,x\) and the circle \(x^2+y^2=4\).
options: B) \(\tfrac{8\pi}{3}+4\sqrt3;\ \tfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
C) \(\tfrac{8\pi}{3}-4\sqrt3;\ \tfrac{4\pi}{3}\)
D) \(\tfrac{4\pi}{3}+2\sqrt3;\ \tfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\tfrac{8\pi}{3}+4\sqrt3;\ \tfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
Concept: \(\text{area between a curve and the }x\text{-axis is }\int y\,dx;\ \text{by symmetry the ellipse strip is four times the first-quadrant part, and a sector of angle }\theta\text{ has area }\tfrac12r^2\theta\)
Given: \(a=4,\ b=2;\ |x|\le2;\ r=2,\ \text{line at }60^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(y=2\sqrt{1-x^2/16};\ x=4\sin t\Rightarrow\int\sqrt{1-\sin^2t}\,4\cos t\,dt=4\int\cos^2t\,dt\)
Step 1: \(\text{area}=4\int_0^2 2\sqrt{1-\tfrac{x^2}{16}}\,dx=32\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos^2t\,dt\)
Step 2: \(32\left[\tfrac t2+\tfrac{\sin2t}{4}\right]_0^{\pi/6}=32\left(\tfrac{\pi}{12}+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{8}\right)=\tfrac{8\pi}{3}+4\sqrt3\)
Step 3: \(\tan\theta=\sqrt3\Rightarrow\theta=\tfrac\pi3;\ \tfrac12(4)\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos^2t\,dt=\left[\frac t2+\frac{\sin2t}{4}\right]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac{\pi}{12}+\frac{\sqrt3}{8}\]
Check: \[\tfrac{8\pi}{3}+4\sqrt3\approx8.38+6.93=15.3<\pi ab=8\pi\approx25.1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the substitution }x=4\sin t\text{ turns the square root into }\cos t\text{, and the limits }x=0,2\text{ become }t=0,\pi/6\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{whole ellipse; sector angle wrong}\); (C) \(\text{sign of the }\sin2t\text{ term wrong; sector doubled}\); (D) \(\text{symmetry factor halved}\).
Key point: \(x=a\sin t\text{ for ellipse areas};\ \text{sector}=\tfrac12r^2\theta\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a homogeneous first-order differential equation by the substitution y = vx and finding the particular solution through a given point
questions.question: Solve \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+y}{x}\) and find the particular solution through \((1,2)\). Find also the general solution of \((x^2+y^2)\,dx-2xy\,dy=0\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(y=x\ln|x|+2x;\ x^2-y^2=Cx\)
Concept: \(\text{if }\frac{dy}{dx}=g\left(\frac yx\right),\ \text{the substitution }y=vx\text{ separates the variables}\)
Given: \(\text{point }(1,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(y=vx\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\)
Step 1: \(v+xv'=1+v\Rightarrow dv=\dfrac{dx}{x}\Rightarrow v=\ln|x|+C\Rightarrow y=x\ln|x|+Cx\)
Step 2: \((1,2):\ 2=0+C\Rightarrow y=x\ln|x|+2x\)
Step 3: \(v+xv'=\dfrac{1+v^2}{2v}\Rightarrow\dfrac{2v\,dv}{1-v^2}=\dfrac{dx}{x}\Rightarrow x(1-v^2)=C\Rightarrow x^2-y^2=Cx\)
Worked derivation: \[-\ln|1-v^2|=\ln|x|+c\Rightarrow x\left(1-\frac{y^2}{x^2}\right)=C\Rightarrow x^2-y^2=Cx\]
Check: \[y=x\ln x+2x:\ y'=\ln x+1+2=\frac{x+y}{x}=1+\ln x+2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{both right-hand sides depend only on }y/x,\ \text{so }y=vx\text{ separates them}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{factor }x\text{ lost; sign wrong}\); (C) \(\text{second solution wrong}\); (D) \(\text{log term missing}\).
Key point: \(y=vx\text{ for homogeneous equations}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the size of a set from its power set, counting subsets with inclusion and exclusion conditions, and intersecting intervals on the number line
questions.question: If the power set of \(A\) has 64 elements, find \(n(A)\). How many subsets of \(\{1,2,\dots,10\}\) contain 1 but not 2? Find \((2,5]\cap[3,7)\) and say how it appears on the number line.
options: D) \(n(A)=6;\ 256;\ [3,5],\ \text{a closed segment from 3 to 5 with both end points included}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(n(A)=6;\ 256;\ [3,5]\)
Concept: \(\text{a set with }n\text{ elements has }2^n\text{ subsets, since each element is either in or out}\)
Given: \(n(P(A))=64;\ \{1,\dots,10\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(n(P(A))=2^{n(A)}\)
Step 1: \(2^n=64\Rightarrow n=6\)
Step 2: \(1\text{ fixed in, }2\text{ fixed out; remaining 8 free}\Rightarrow2^8=256\)
Step 3: \((2,5]\cap[3,7)=\{x:3\le x\le5\}=[3,5]\)
Worked derivation: \[\max(2,3)=3\text{ (included in }[3,7)\text{ and in }(2,5]),\ \ \min(5,7)=5\text{ (included in }(2,5]\text{ and }[3,7))\]
Check: \[2^{10}=1024\text{ subsets in all; one quarter fix the status of 1 and 2 as required: }1024/4=256\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{fixing elements removes their two-way choices}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2^8=256;\ \text{end points included}\); (B) \(2^6=64;\ \text{union taken}\); (C) \(\text{count and interval wrong}\).
Key point: \(n(P(A))=2^n\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Testing relations for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity, identifying equivalence classes of congruence modulo 5, and counting equivalence relations on a small set
questions.question: Which statement about relations is correct?
options: A) \(R=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:5\mid(a-b)\}\text{ is an equivalence relation with exactly 5 equivalence classes }[0],[1],[2],[3],[4];\ \text{"}a\le b\text{" on }\mathbb R\text{ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric};\ \text{"is perpendicular to" on lines in a plane is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive};\ \text{exactly 2 equivalence relations on }\{1,2,3\}\text{ contain }(1,2)\)
B) \(\text{"}a\le b\text{" is an equivalence relation}\)
C) \(5\mid(a-b)\text{ gives infinitely many equivalence classes}\)
D) \(\text{"is perpendicular to" is transitive}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\text{congruence mod 5 has 5 classes; properties of }\le\text{ and }\perp\text{ correct; 2 equivalence relations}\)
Concept: \(\text{an equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and it splits the set into disjoint equivalence classes}\)
Given: \(\text{relations on }\mathbb Z,\ \mathbb R,\ \text{lines},\ \{1,2,3\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{reflexive }(a,a);\ \text{symmetric }(a,b)\Rightarrow(b,a);\ \text{transitive }(a,b),(b,c)\Rightarrow(a,c)\)
Step 1: \(5\mid0;\ 5\mid(a-b)\Rightarrow5\mid(b-a);\ 5\mid(a-b),5\mid(b-c)\Rightarrow5\mid(a-c)\Rightarrow\text{classes by remainder }0\text{–}4\)
Step 2: \(\le:\ a\le a,\ a\le b\le c\Rightarrow a\le c,\ \text{but }1\le2\not\Rightarrow2\le1;\ \perp:\ L_1\perp L_2\Rightarrow L_2\perp L_1,\ L\not\perp L,\ L_1\perp L_2\perp L_3\Rightarrow L_1\parallel L_3\)
Step 3: \(\text{partitions with 1, 2 together: }\{\{1,2\},\{3\}\},\ \{\{1,2,3\}\}\Rightarrow2\)
Worked derivation: \[a-b=5m,\ b-c=5n\Rightarrow a-c=5(m+n)\]
Check: \[\text{every integer has exactly one remainder in }\{0,1,2,3,4\}\text{ on division by 5}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{equivalence relations correspond to partitions, so counting them means counting partitions}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\le\text{ is not symmetric}\); (C) \(\text{only 5 remainders}\); (D) \(\text{two perpendiculars to the same line are parallel}\).
Key point: \(\text{equivalence}=\text{R + S + T}\Leftrightarrow\text{partition}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using sum-to-product formulae to count solutions of a trigonometric equation on an interval and to evaluate sums and differences of sines and cosines
questions.question: How many solutions does \(\sin x+\sin3x=0\) have in \([0,\pi]\)? Evaluate \(\cos75^\circ+\cos15^\circ\) and \(\sin75^\circ-\sin15^\circ\).
options: A) \(2;\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2};\ \tfrac12\)
B) \(3\ (x=0,\tfrac\pi2,\pi);\ \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2};\ \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\)
C) \(4;\ \sqrt2;\ \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\)
D) \(3;\ \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2};\ \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(3\text{ solutions};\ \tfrac{\sqrt6}2;\ \tfrac{\sqrt2}2\)
Concept: \(\sin C+\sin D=2\sin\tfrac{C+D}2\cos\tfrac{C-D}2;\ \cos C+\cos D=2\cos\tfrac{C+D}2\cos\tfrac{C-D}2;\ \sin C-\sin D=2\cos\tfrac{C+D}2\sin\tfrac{C-D}2\)
Given: \(x\in[0,\pi]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{sum-to-product identities}\)
Step 1: \(\sin3x+\sin x=2\sin2x\cos x=0\)
Step 2: \(\sin2x=0\Rightarrow x=0,\tfrac\pi2,\pi;\ \cos x=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac\pi2\Rightarrow\text{distinct: }3\)
Step 3: \(2\cos45^\circ\cos30^\circ=2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=\tfrac{\sqrt6}2;\ 2\cos45^\circ\sin30^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin3x+\sin x=2\sin\frac{3x+x}{2}\cos\frac{3x-x}{2}=2\sin2x\cos x\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac\pi2:\ \sin\tfrac\pi2+\sin\tfrac{3\pi}2=1-1=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{converting the sum to a product lets each factor be set to zero}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{values and count wrong}\); (C) \(\pi/2\text{ counted twice}\); (D) \(\text{values swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{sum}\to\text{product, then count distinct roots}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding an unknown coefficient from a condition on the difference of roots or equal roots, and evaluating symmetric functions of roots
questions.question: Find \(p\) if the roots of \(x^2-px+12=0\) differ by 1, and \(k\) if \(x^2+kx+9=0\) has equal roots. If \(\alpha,\beta\) are roots of \(2x^2-5x+3=0\), find \(\alpha^2+\beta^2\).
options: B) \(p=7\text{ only};\ k=6\text{ only};\ \tfrac{19}{4}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(p=\pm7;\ k=\pm6;\ \alpha^2+\beta^2=\tfrac{13}{4}\)
Concept: \(\text{for }ax^2+bx+c=0:\ \alpha+\beta=-\tfrac ba,\ \alpha\beta=\tfrac ca,\ (\alpha-\beta)^2=\tfrac{b^2-4ac}{a^2};\ \text{equal roots}\Leftrightarrow D=0\)
Given: \(|\alpha-\beta|=1;\ D=0\)
Formula/Principle: \((\alpha-\beta)^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta\)
Step 1: \(p^2-48=1\Rightarrow p=\pm7\)
Step 2: \(k^2-36=0\Rightarrow k=\pm6\)
Step 3: \(\alpha^2+\beta^2=\left(\tfrac52\right)^2-2\cdot\tfrac32=\tfrac{25}{4}-3=\tfrac{13}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[p=7:\ x^2-7x+12=(x-3)(x-4),\ \text{roots differ by }1\]
Check: \[\alpha=1,\ \beta=\tfrac32:\ 1+\tfrac94=\tfrac{13}{4}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{conditions on roots become conditions on coefficients through Vieta's relations}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{discriminant conditions misapplied}\); (B) \(\text{negative values also work}\); (D) \(p^2=49,\ k^2=36\).
Key point: \((\alpha-\beta)^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-4\alpha\beta\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the range of a parameter for which a cubic has three distinct real roots using the values at its turning points, and the limiting case of a repeated root
questions.question: For what values of \(k\) does \(x^3-3x+k=0\) have three distinct real roots? What are the roots when \(k=2\)? How many real roots has \(x^4+x^2+1=0\)?
options: C) \(-2<k<2;\ x=1\text{ (double)},\ x=-2;\ 0\ \text{real roots, since }x^4+x^2+1\ge1\)
D) \(k<-2;\ \text{one real root};\ 0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(-2<k<2;\ \text{roots }1,1,-2;\ \text{no real roots}\)
Concept: \(\text{a cubic has three distinct real roots exactly when its local maximum is positive and its local minimum is negative}\)
Given: \(f(x)=x^3-3x+k\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(x)=3x^2-3=0\Rightarrow x=\pm1;\ f(-1)>0>f(1)\)
Step 1: \(f(-1)=k+2,\ f(1)=k-2\)
Step 2: \(k+2>0\text{ and }k-2<0\Rightarrow-2<k<2\)
Step 3: \(k=2:\ x^3-3x+2=(x-1)^2(x+2)\Rightarrow1,1,-2\)
Worked derivation: \[(x-1)^2(x+2)=(x^2-2x+1)(x+2)=x^3-3x+2\]
Check: \[x^4+x^2+1=\left(x^2+\tfrac12\right)^2+\tfrac34>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at the boundary }k=\pm2\text{ a turning point touches the axis, giving a repeated root}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only one real root for }k>2\); (B) \(\text{boundary gives repeated roots; quartic has none}\); (D) \(\text{range wrong}\).
Key point: \(f(x_{\max})>0>f(x_{\min})\Leftrightarrow3\text{ distinct real roots}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the distance of closest approach of an alpha particle to a gold nucleus, how it scales with kinetic energy and nuclear charge, and what the scattering observations imply
questions.question: A \(5.0\text{ MeV}\) alpha particle is fired head-on at a gold nucleus (\(Z=79\); take \(\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=1.44\text{ MeV fm}\)). Find the distance of closest approach, how it changes if the energy is doubled, and the correct conclusion from the Geiger–Marsden experiment.
options: A) \(45.5\text{ fm}\ (\approx4.6\times10^{-14}\text{ m});\ \text{halves};\ \text{most alpha particles pass undeflected and only about 1 in 8000 is deflected by more than }90^\circ,\ \text{so the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus; the number scattered at angle }\theta\text{ varies as }1/\sin^4(\theta/2)\)
B) \(91\text{ fm};\ \text{doubles};\ \text{positive charge is spread uniformly through the atom}\)
C) \(22.8\text{ fm};\ \text{unchanged};\ \text{most alpha particles bounce straight back}\)
D) \(45.5\text{ fm};\ \text{quarters};\ \text{electrons cause the large-angle scattering}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(r_0\approx45.5\text{ fm};\ r_0\propto1/K\Rightarrow\text{halves};\ \text{tiny massive nucleus}\)
Given: \(K=5.0\text{ MeV},\ Z=79,\ ze=2e\)
Formula/Principle: \(K=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_0}\Rightarrow r_0=\dfrac{2Z\,(e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0)}{K}\)
Step 1: \(2Z\times1.44=2\times79\times1.44=227.5\text{ MeV fm}\)
Step 2: \(r_0=\dfrac{227.5}{5.0}=45.5\text{ fm}\)
Step 3: \(K\to2K\Rightarrow r_0\to\tfrac12r_0=22.8\text{ fm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{at closest approach (head-on) all kinetic energy becomes electric potential energy: } \frac12mv^2=\frac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0}\]
Check: \[r_0=45.5\ \text{fm}\gg R_{\text{Au}}\approx1.2(197)^{1/3}\approx7\ \text{fm, so the alpha never touches the nucleus}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only a concentrated positive charge can turn back a fast, heavy alpha particle}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{factor 2 error; }r_0\propto1/K\); (C) \(r_0\text{ depends on }K;\ \text{most pass undeflected}\); (D) \(r_0\propto1/K,\ \text{not }1/K^2\).
Key point: \(r_0=\dfrac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0K};\ \text{nucleus tiny and massive}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the numbers of protons and neutrons and the radius of a nucleus from its symbol, finding the mass number of a nucleus of half that radius, and classifying isotopes, isobars and isotones
questions.question: For \(^{64}_{29}\text{Cu}\) (\(R_0=1.2\text{ fm}\)), find the numbers of protons and neutrons and its radius, and the mass number of a nucleus with half this radius. Among \(^{12}_{6}\text{C},\ ^{14}_{6}\text{C},\ ^{14}_{7}\text{N},\ ^{16}_{8}\text{O}\), identify isotopes, isobars and isotones. Which statement about the nuclear force is correct?
options: A) \(29\text{ p},\ 64\text{ n};\ 9.6\text{ fm};\ A=32;\ \text{isotopes }^{14}\text{C},^{14}\text{N}\)
B) \(35\text{ p},\ 29\text{ n};\ 4.8\text{ fm};\ A=16;\ \text{nuclear force acts only between protons}\)
C) \(29\text{ p},\ 35\text{ n};\ 4.8\text{ fm};\ A=32;\ \text{isotones }^{12}\text{C},^{14}\text{N};\ \text{nuclear force is long-ranged}\)

D) \(29\text{ p},\ 35\text{ n};\ 4.8\text{ fm};\ A=8;\ \text{isotopes }^{12}\text{C},^{14}\text{C}\ (\text{same }Z),\ \text{isobars }^{14}\text{C},^{14}\text{N}\ (\text{same }A),\ \text{isotones }^{14}\text{C},^{16}\text{O}\ (\text{8 neutrons each});\ \text{the nuclear force is attractive, short-ranged, nearly the same for p–p, n–n and n–p pairs, and saturates, so binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant for medium nuclei}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(29\text{ p},\ 35\text{ n};\ R=4.8\text{ fm};\ A=8;\ \text{classification and nuclear force correct}\)
Given: \(Z=29,\ A=64,\ R_0=1.2\text{ fm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(N=A-Z;\ R=R_0A^{1/3}\Rightarrow A\propto R^3\)
Step 1: \(N=64-29=35\)
Step 2: \(R=1.2\times64^{1/3}=1.2\times4=4.8\text{ fm}\)
Step 3: \(R\to\tfrac R2\Rightarrow A\to\tfrac{64}{8}=8\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{A_2}{A_1}=\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^3=\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac18\]
Check: \[^{14}_6\text{C}:\ N=8;\ ^{16}_8\text{O}:\ N=8\Rightarrow\text{isotones}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{nuclear volume is proportional to the number of nucleons, so halving the radius divides }A\text{ by 8}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(N=A-Z;\ ^{14}\text{C and }^{14}\text{N are isobars}\); (B) \(Z\text{ and }N\text{ swapped}\); (C) \(A=8;\ ^{12}\text{C has 6 and }^{14}\text{N has 7 neutrons}\).
Key point: \(N=A-Z;\ A\propto R^3;\ \text{isotopes }Z,\ \text{isobars }A,\ \text{isotones }N\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating electron and hole densities in silicon doped with a pentavalent impurity using the mass-action law, and reading how resistivity of a semiconductor varies with temperature
questions.question: Pure silicon has \(n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\text{ m}^{-3}\). It is doped with arsenic at \(5\times10^{22}\text{ atoms m}^{-3}\). Find \(n_e\) and \(n_h\), the type of semiconductor, and the shape of its resistivity–temperature graph.
options: A) \(n_e=n_h=1.5\times10^{16};\ \text{intrinsic};\ \text{resistivity rises with }T\)

B) \(n_e\approx5\times10^{22}\text{ m}^{-3},\ n_h=\dfrac{n_i^2}{n_e}=4.5\times10^9\text{ m}^{-3};\ \text{n-type (arsenic is a pentavalent donor)};\ \text{resistivity falls with rising temperature as more electron–hole pairs are produced}\)
C) \(n_h=5\times10^{22},\ n_e=4.5\times10^9;\ \text{p-type};\ \text{resistivity constant}\)
D) \(n_e=5\times10^{22},\ n_h=5\times10^{22};\ \text{n-type};\ \text{resistivity rises linearly}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(n_e\approx5\times10^{22},\ n_h=4.5\times10^9\text{ m}^{-3};\ \text{n-type};\ \rho\text{ decreases with }T\)
Given: \(n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\text{ m}^{-3},\ N_D=5\times10^{22}\text{ m}^{-3}\)
Formula/Principle: \(n_en_h=n_i^2;\ n_e\approx N_D\ (N_D\gg n_i)\)
Step 1: \(\text{As has 5 valence electrons}\Rightarrow\text{donor}\Rightarrow n_e\approx5\times10^{22}\text{ m}^{-3}\)
Step 2: \(n_i^2=2.25\times10^{32}\)
Step 3: \(n_h=\dfrac{2.25\times10^{32}}{5\times10^{22}}=4.5\times10^9\text{ m}^{-3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{n_e}{n_h}=\frac{5\times10^{22}}{4.5\times10^{9}}\approx1.1\times10^{13}\Rightarrow\text{electrons are the majority carriers}\]
Check: \[n_en_h=5\times10^{22}\times4.5\times10^9=2.25\times10^{32}=n_i^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{donors add electrons, and more electrons recombine with holes, cutting the hole density far below }n_i\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{doping changes carrier densities; }\rho\text{ falls}\); (C) \(\text{arsenic gives n-type}\); (D) \(\text{mass-action law violated}\).
Key point: \(n_en_h=n_i^2;\ \text{pentavalent}\Rightarrow\text{n-type}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding average velocity over an interval and instantaneous velocity from a position–time relation measured by a motion sensor, and distinguishing average speed from average velocity
questions.question: A motion sensor records a trolley's position as \(x=2t^2+3t\) (metres, seconds). Find the average velocity between \(t=1\text{ s}\) and \(t=3\text{ s}\) and the instantaneous velocity at \(t=2\text{ s}\). A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track in 80 s; find the average speed and average velocity.
options: C) \(11\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 11\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 5\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 0\ (\text{zero displacement}) — \text{for uniform acceleration the average velocity over an interval equals the instantaneous velocity at its midpoint}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(11\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 11\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 5\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 0\)
Given: \(x(t)=2t^2+3t;\ \text{lap }400\text{ m in }80\text{ s}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar v=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t};\ v=\dfrac{dx}{dt};\ \text{average speed}=\dfrac{\text{path length}}{\text{time}}\)
Step 1: \(x(3)=18+9=27,\ x(1)=2+3=5\Rightarrow\bar v=\dfrac{22}{2}=11\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(v=4t+3\Rightarrow v(2)=11\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(\text{speed}=400/80=5\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{displacement }0\Rightarrow\bar v=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\bar v=\frac{x(t_2)-x(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}=2(t_1+t_2)+3=v\!\left(\frac{t_1+t_2}{2}\right)\]
Check: \[2(1+3)+3=11=v(2)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{velocity depends on displacement, speed on total path length}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgot to divide by }\Delta t;\ \text{lap displacement is }0\); (B) \(\text{arithmetic errors; values swapped}\); (D) \(v(2)=4(2)+3=11\).
Key point: \(\bar v=\Delta x/\Delta t;\ v=dx/dt\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Analysing a projectile launched upward at an angle from the top of a building to find its time of flight, horizontal range and speed on hitting the ground
questions.question: A ball is thrown from the top of an 80 m tall building with speed \(50\text{ m s}^{-1}\) at \(37^\circ\) above the horizontal (\(\sin37^\circ=0.6,\ \cos37^\circ=0.8,\ g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). Find the time to reach the ground, the horizontal distance from the building, the maximum height above the ground and the speed on impact.
options: D) \(8\text{ s};\ 320\text{ m};\ 125\text{ m};\ \sqrt{4100}\approx64\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(8\text{ s};\ 320\text{ m};\ 125\text{ m};\ \approx64\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Given: \(u_x=40,\ u_y=30\text{ m s}^{-1};\ h=80\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(y=u_yt-\tfrac12gt^2;\ x=u_xt;\ H=\dfrac{u_y^2}{2g}\)
Step 1: \(-80=30t-5t^2\Rightarrow t^2-6t-16=0\Rightarrow(t-8)(t+2)=0\Rightarrow t=8\text{ s}\)
Step 2: \(x=40\times8=320\text{ m};\ H=80+\dfrac{900}{20}=125\text{ m}\)
Step 3: \(v_y=30-80=-50,\ v_x=40\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{1600+2500}=\sqrt{4100}\approx64.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[v^2=u^2+2gh=2500+2(10)(80)=4100\ (\text{energy conservation})\]
Check: \[\text{fall from }125\text{ m: }\sqrt{2(10)(125)}=50=|v_y|\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the vertical motion alone fixes the flight time; horizontal velocity stays constant}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the building height}\); (B) \(\text{time too short}\); (C) \(\text{time too long}\).
Key point: \(\text{solve }y(t)=-h\text{ for }t;\ v^2=u^2+2gh\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding minimum speeds at the top and bottom of a vertical circle for a mass on a string and the difference in string tension between bottom and top
questions.question: A student whirls a \(0.50\text{ kg}\) bucket of water in a vertical circle of radius \(1.0\text{ m}\) on a rope (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). What is the least speed at the top for the water to stay in, the corresponding speed at the bottom, and by how much the rope tension at the bottom exceeds that at the top for any speed?
options: B) \(\sqrt{10}\approx3.2\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \sqrt{50}\approx7.1\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 6mg=30\text{ N}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(v_{\text{top}}=\sqrt{gr}\approx3.2\text{ m s}^{-1};\ v_{\text{bottom}}=\sqrt{5gr}\approx7.1\text{ m s}^{-1};\ T_b-T_t=6mg=30\text{ N}\)
Given: \(m=0.50\text{ kg},\ r=1.0\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{top: }T+mg=\dfrac{mv_t^2}{r};\ \text{bottom: }T-mg=\dfrac{mv_b^2}{r};\ v_b^2=v_t^2+4gr\)
Step 1: \(T_t=0\Rightarrow v_t=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{10}\)
Step 2: \(v_b^2=10+40=50\Rightarrow v_b=\sqrt{50}\)
Step 3: \(T_b-T_t=\dfrac{m(v_b^2-v_t^2)}{r}+2mg=4mg+2mg=6mg=30\text{ N}\)
Worked derivation: \[\tfrac12mv_b^2=\tfrac12mv_t^2+mg(2r)\Rightarrow v_b^2-v_t^2=4gr\]
Check: \[\text{at minimum speed }T_b=\frac{0.5\times50}{1}+5=30\ \text{N},\ T_t=0\Rightarrow\text{difference }30\ \text{N}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at the top gravity alone must supply the centripetal force when the rope just goes slack}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{a rope cannot push, so }v_t\ne0\); (C) \(\text{forgot square roots}\); (D) \(v_b^2=v_t^2+4gr\).
Key point: \(v_t\ge\sqrt{gr};\ v_b\ge\sqrt{5gr};\ T_b-T_t=6mg\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing escape speeds for planets of different radius and density, and calculating the energy needed to raise a body to a height equal to the Earth's radius
questions.question: Escape speed from Earth is \(11.2\text{ km s}^{-1}\). Find the escape speed from (i) a planet of the same density but twice Earth's radius, (ii) a planet of Earth's mass but half its radius. How much energy is needed to raise a 100 kg body from Earth's surface to a height \(R_E=6.4\times10^6\text{ m}\) (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\))?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(22.4\text{ and }15.8\text{ km s}^{-1};\ 3.2\times10^9\text{ J}\)
Given: \(v_e=11.2\text{ km s}^{-1};\ m=100\text{ kg},\ h=R_E\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_e=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}=R\sqrt{\tfrac83\pi G\rho};\ U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}\)
Step 1: \(\rho\text{ same},\ R\to2R\Rightarrow v_e\to2v_e=22.4\text{ km s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(M\text{ same},\ R\to\tfrac R2\Rightarrow v_e\to\sqrt2\,v_e=15.8\text{ km s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(\Delta U=GMm\left(\dfrac1R-\dfrac1{2R}\right)=\dfrac{mgR}{2}=\dfrac{100\times10\times6.4\times10^6}{2}=3.2\times10^9\text{ J}\)
Worked derivation: \[M=\tfrac43\pi R^3\rho\Rightarrow\frac{2GM}{R}=\tfrac83\pi G\rho R^2\Rightarrow v_e\propto R\sqrt\rho\]
Check: \[mgh=6.4\times10^9\ \text{J overestimates because }g\text{ falls with height; the exact value is half}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{escape speed depends on }M/R,\ \text{and potential energy varies as }1/r,\ \text{not linearly with height}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores dependence on }R;\ mgh\text{ invalid for large }h\); (B) \(\text{scalings inverted}\); (D) \(\text{scalings swapped}\).
Key point: \(v_e\propto R\sqrt\rho;\ \Delta U=GMm(1/r_1-1/r_2)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the terminal velocity of a steel ball falling through a viscous liquid using Stokes' law, the viscous force at terminal velocity, and how terminal velocity scales with radius
questions.question: A steel ball of radius \(1.0\text{ mm}\) (density \(7800\text{ kg m}^{-3}\)) falls through glycerine (density \(1200\text{ kg m}^{-3}\), viscosity \(1.0\text{ Pa s}\)), \(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Find its terminal velocity, the viscous force on it at terminal velocity, and the terminal velocity of a ball of radius 2.0 mm.
options: D) \(1.47\times10^{-2}\text{ m s}^{-1}\ (\approx1.5\text{ cm s}^{-1});\ 2.8\times10^{-4}\text{ N};\ 5.9\times10^{-2}\text{ m s}^{-1}\ (\text{four times, since }v_t\propto r^2)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(v_t\approx1.47\times10^{-2}\text{ m s}^{-1};\ F\approx2.8\times10^{-4}\text{ N};\ 5.9\times10^{-2}\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Given: \(r=1.0\times10^{-3}\text{ m},\ \rho=7800,\ \sigma=1200,\ \eta=1.0\)
Formula/Principle: \(F=6\pi\eta rv;\ v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}\)
Step 1: \(v_t=\dfrac{2\times10^{-6}\times6600\times10}{9\times1.0}=\dfrac{0.132}{9}=1.47\times10^{-2}\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(F=6\pi(1.0)(10^{-3})(1.47\times10^{-2})=2.77\times10^{-4}\text{ N}\)
Step 3: \(r\to2r\Rightarrow v_t\to4v_t=5.9\times10^{-2}\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[6\pi\eta rv_t=\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho-\sigma)g\Rightarrow v_t=\frac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}\]
Check: \[\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho-\sigma)g=4.19\times10^{-9}\times6600\times10=2.77\times10^{-4}\ \text{N}=F\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at terminal velocity viscous drag balances weight minus buoyancy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{off by }10^2\); (B) \(\text{buoyancy ignored}\); (C) \(v_t\propto r^2,\ \text{not }r\).
Key point: \(v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}\propto r^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Explaining heat conduction through rods in series and parallel, finding the junction temperature and effective conductivity, and everyday consequences of thermal conductivity
questions.question: Two rods of equal length and area, with conductivities \(K\) and \(2K\), are joined end to end; the free ends are kept at \(100^\circ\text{C}\) and \(0^\circ\text{C}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) In steady state the same heat current flows through both rods, so \(K(100-T)=2K(T-0)\) gives a junction temperature \(T\approx33.3^\circ\text{C}\); the effective conductivity in series is \(\dfrac{2K\cdot K\cdot2}{K+2K}=\dfrac43K\), while side by side (parallel) it would be \(\dfrac{K+2K}{2}=1.5K\); metals feel colder than wood at the same temperature because their high conductivity draws heat quickly from the hand, and cooking pots have copper bottoms to spread heat rapidly
B) The junction is at \(50^\circ\text{C}\) because the rods have equal length
C) More heat flows through the rod of higher conductivity even in series; the junction is at \(66.7^\circ\text{C}\)
D) Metals feel colder because they are at a lower temperature than wood in the same room
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(T\approx33.3^\circ\text{C};\ K_{\text{series}}=\tfrac43K,\ K_{\text{parallel}}=1.5K;\ \text{everyday effects correctly explained}\)
Given: \(K_1=K,\ K_2=2K;\ \text{equal }L,\ A;\ 100^\circ\text{C},\ 0^\circ\text{C}\)
Formula/Principle: \(H=\dfrac{KA\Delta T}{L};\ \text{series: same }H;\ R_{\text{th}}=\dfrac{L}{KA}\text{ add}\)
Step 1: \(K(100-T)=2K\,T\Rightarrow3T=100\Rightarrow T=33.3^\circ\text{C}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{2L}{K_{\text{eq}}A}=\dfrac{L}{KA}+\dfrac{L}{2KA}\Rightarrow K_{\text{eq}}=\dfrac43K\)
Step 3: \(\text{parallel: }K_{\text{eq}}\cdot2A=KA+2KA\Rightarrow K_{\text{eq}}=1.5K\)
Worked derivation: \[H=\frac{KA(100-33.3)}{L}=\frac{2KA(33.3-0)}{L}=66.7\frac{KA}{L}\]
Check: \[\text{temperature drop is larger across the poorer conductor: }66.7^\circ\text{ vs }33.3^\circ\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in series the heat current must be continuous, so the lower-conductivity rod needs the larger temperature drop}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{equal lengths do not mean equal drops}\); (C) \(\text{series rods carry equal current; junction at }33.3^\circ\text{C}\); (D) \(\text{both are at room temperature}\).
Key point: \(\text{series: same }H,\ \Delta T\propto1/K\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating efficiency, work output and heat rejected for a Carnot engine, its change when the sink temperature is lowered, and the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements of the second law
questions.question: A Carnot engine works between \(600\text{ K}\) and \(400\text{ K}\) and absorbs \(1200\text{ J}\) per cycle. Find its efficiency, work per cycle and heat rejected. What is the efficiency if the sink is lowered to \(300\text{ K}\)? Which statement of the second law is correct?
options: A) \(66.7\%;\ 800\text{ J};\ 400\text{ J};\ 75\%;\ \text{a perfect engine is possible}\)
B) \(33.3\%;\ 400\text{ J};\ 1600\text{ J};\ 50\%;\ \text{heat flows spontaneously from cold to hot}\)

D) \(33.3\%;\ 400\text{ J};\ 800\text{ J};\ 50\%;\ \text{Kelvin–Planck: no engine can convert all absorbed heat into work in a cycle; Clausius: no process can transfer heat from a colder to a hotter body without external work}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\eta=\tfrac13;\ W=400\text{ J};\ Q_2=800\text{ J};\ \eta'=50\%\)
Given: \(T_1=600\text{ K},\ T_2=400\text{ K},\ Q_1=1200\text{ J}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1};\ W=\eta Q_1;\ Q_2=Q_1-W\)
Step 1: \(\eta=1-\tfrac{400}{600}=\tfrac13\)
Step 2: \(W=400\text{ J};\ Q_2=800\text{ J}\)
Step 3: \(T_2=300\text{ K}:\ \eta'=1-\tfrac{300}{600}=\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}=\frac{T_2}{T_1}\Rightarrow Q_2=1200\times\frac{400}{600}=800\ \text{J}\]
Check: \[Q_1=W+Q_2=400+800=1200\ \text{J}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a Carnot engine's efficiency depends only on the two reservoir temperatures}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{used }T_2/T_1\text{ as efficiency; perfect engines are impossible}\); (B) \(Q_2<Q_1;\ \text{heat does not flow cold to hot unaided}\); (C) \(\text{efficiency wrong}\).
Key point: \(\eta=1-T_2/T_1;\ Q_2/Q_1=T_2/T_1\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using energy conservation to find the speed and string tension at the lowest point of a pendulum released from an angle, and the small-angle period on Earth and the Moon
questions.question: A pendulum bob of mass \(m\) on a \(1.0\text{ m}\) string is released from rest at \(60^\circ\) to the vertical (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). Find the speed and tension at the lowest point, the small-amplitude period, and the period on the Moon (\(g_M=g/6\)).
options: A) \(\sqrt{10}\approx3.2\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 2mg;\ 2.0\text{ s};\ \approx4.9\text{ s}\)
C) \(\sqrt5\text{ m s}^{-1};\ mg;\ 2.0\text{ s};\ 0.8\text{ s}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(v=\sqrt{10}\text{ m s}^{-1};\ T=2mg;\ 2.0\text{ s};\ \approx4.9\text{ s}\)
Given: \(L=1.0\text{ m},\ \theta_0=60^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tfrac12mv^2=mgL(1-\cos\theta_0);\ T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{L};\ T_p=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\)
Step 1: \(v^2=2gL(1-\tfrac12)=gL=10\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{10}\approx3.2\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(T=mg+\dfrac{m\cdot10}{1}=2mg\)
Step 3: \(T_p=2\pi\sqrt{0.1}=1.99\text{ s};\ \text{Moon: }\sqrt6\times1.99\approx4.9\text{ s}\)
Worked derivation: \[T=mg+\frac{m\cdot2gL(1-\cos\theta_0)}{L}=mg(3-2\cos\theta_0)=mg(3-1)=2mg\]
Check: \[2\pi\sqrt{1/10}=2\pi\times0.316=1.99\ \text{s}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the height fallen sets the speed, and the string must supply the centripetal force in addition to supporting the weight}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{speed and tension wrong; period scales by }\sqrt6\); (C) \(\text{speed wrong; Moon period is longer}\); (D) \(T=2mg;\ \text{period wrong}\).
Key point: \(T_{\text{bottom}}=mg(3-2\cos\theta_0);\ T_p\propto1/\sqrt g\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the fundamental frequency and allowed harmonics of open and closed organ pipes of the same length and finding the length of a closed pipe in resonance with an open one
questions.question: An open pipe and a closed pipe are each \(0.85\text{ m}\) long (speed of sound \(340\text{ m s}^{-1}\)). Find each fundamental frequency and the first two overtones of each. How long must a closed pipe be for its fundamental to equal the open pipe's fundamental?
options: A) \(\text{open }100\text{ Hz};\ \text{closed }200\text{ Hz};\ 1.7\text{ m}\)
B) \(\text{open }200\text{ Hz (overtones }400,600\text{)};\ \text{closed }100\text{ Hz (overtones }300,500\text{ — odd harmonics only)};\ 0.425\text{ m}\)
C) \(\text{both }200\text{ Hz};\ \text{all harmonics in both};\ 0.85\text{ m}\)
D) \(\text{open }200\text{ Hz (overtones }300,400\text{)};\ \text{closed }100\text{ Hz (overtones }200,300\text{)};\ 0.85\text{ m}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\text{open }200\text{ Hz};\ 400,600;\ \text{closed }100\text{ Hz};\ 300,500;\ 0.425\text{ m}\)
Given: \(L=0.85\text{ m},\ v=340\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{open: }f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}\ (n=1,2,3\dots);\ \text{closed: }f_n=\dfrac{nv}{4L}\ (n=1,3,5\dots)\)
Step 1: \(\text{open: }\dfrac{340}{1.7}=200\text{ Hz};\ 400,\ 600\text{ Hz}\)
Step 2: \(\text{closed: }\dfrac{340}{3.4}=100\text{ Hz};\ 300,\ 500\text{ Hz}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{v}{4L'}=200\Rightarrow L'=\dfrac{340}{800}=0.425\text{ m}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{closed end = node, open end = antinode}\Rightarrow L=(2n-1)\frac\lambda4;\quad\text{both ends open}\Rightarrow L=n\frac\lambda2\]
Check: \[\text{closed pipe of }0.425\text{ m: }\frac{340}{4\times0.425}=200\ \text{Hz}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a closed end forces a node, allowing only odd quarter-wavelength fits}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{fundamentals swapped}\); (C) \(\text{closed pipe has half the frequency and odd harmonics only}\); (D) \(\text{overtones wrong}\).
Key point: \(\text{open: }nv/2L\text{ all }n;\ \text{closed: }nv/4L\text{ odd }n\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying Gauss's theorem to find total and per-face electric flux through a cube with a charge at its centre and at a corner, and the net flux of a uniform field through a closed surface
questions.question: A charge \(q=8.85\times10^{-9}\text{ C}\) is placed (i) at the centre of a cube, (ii) at one corner of the cube (\(\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{ N}^{-1}\text{ m}^{-2}\)). Find the total flux through the cube and through one face in case (i), and the flux through the cube in case (ii). What is the net flux of a uniform field through any closed surface with no charge inside?
options: C) \(1000\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1};\ 166.7\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1};\ 125\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1}\ (\text{one-eighth});\ 0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(1000;\ 166.7;\ 125\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1};\ 0\)
Given: \(q/\varepsilon_0=\dfrac{8.85\times10^{-9}}{8.85\times10^{-12}}=1000\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(\text{centre: total}=1000\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(\text{symmetry: each face }1000/6=166.7\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(\text{corner: the charge is shared by 8 cubes}\Rightarrow1000/8=125\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{8 identical cubes meeting at the corner enclose }q\text{ completely}\Rightarrow\Phi_{\text{one cube}}=\frac{1}{8}\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\]
Check: \[\text{uniform field: flux in through one side equals flux out through the other}\Rightarrow\Phi_{\text{net}}=0=\frac{0}{\varepsilon_0}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{flux through a closed surface depends only on the enclosed charge}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{corner case encloses only }1/8;\ \text{net flux of uniform field is }0\); (B) \(\text{forgot to divide by }\varepsilon_0\); (D) \(\text{corner charge is not fully enclosed}\).
Key point: \(\Phi=q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0;\ \text{use symmetry for parts}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Explaining how charge, potential difference and energy are shared among capacitors in series and parallel, and the equivalent capacitance of each combination
questions.question: A \(2\ \mu\text{F}\) and a \(4\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor are connected (i) in series and (ii) in parallel across a \(12\text{ V}\) battery. Which statement is correct?
options: A) In series both capacitors have the same potential difference, 6 V each
B) In parallel the charge on each is the same, 24 µC
C) In series the equivalent capacitance is \(6\ \mu\text{F}\) and in parallel \(\tfrac43\ \mu\text{F}\)

D) In series \(C_{\text{eq}}=\tfrac43\ \mu\text{F}\), each capacitor carries the same charge \(16\ \mu\text{C}\), and the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage (8 V across \(2\ \mu\text{F}\), 4 V across \(4\ \mu\text{F}\)); in parallel \(C_{\text{eq}}=6\ \mu\text{F}\), both have 12 V, with charges 24 µC and 48 µC; the parallel combination stores more energy (432 µJ against 96 µJ in series)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\text{Series: }\tfrac43\ \mu\text{F},\ 16\ \mu\text{C each},\ 8\text{ V and }4\text{ V};\ \text{parallel: }6\ \mu\text{F},\ 12\text{ V each},\ 24\text{ and }48\ \mu\text{C}\)
Given: \(C_1=2\ \mu\text{F},\ C_2=4\ \mu\text{F},\ V=12\text{ V}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1{C_s}=\dfrac1{C_1}+\dfrac1{C_2};\ C_p=C_1+C_2;\ U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(C_s=\dfrac{2\times4}{6}=\tfrac43\ \mu\text{F};\ Q=\tfrac43\times12=16\ \mu\text{C}\)
Step 2: \(V_1=16/2=8\text{ V},\ V_2=16/4=4\text{ V}\)
Step 3: \(C_p=6\ \mu\text{F};\ Q_1=24,\ Q_2=48\ \mu\text{C};\ U_p=\tfrac12(6)(144)=432\ \mu\text{J},\ U_s=\tfrac12\left(\tfrac43\right)(144)=96\ \mu\text{J}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{series: same }Q,\ V_i=\frac{Q}{C_i};\quad\text{parallel: same }V,\ Q_i=C_iV\]
Check: \[V_1+V_2=8+4=12\ \text{V};\ Q_1+Q_2=72=6\times12\ \mu\text{C}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{series plates are charged by the same current, so charges match; parallel capacitors share the same terminals, so voltages match}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{voltages divide inversely as }C\); (B) \(\text{charges differ in parallel}\); (C) \(\text{formulas swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{series: same }Q;\ \text{parallel: same }V\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Explaining terminal voltage of a cell during discharge and charging, and choosing series or parallel grouping of identical cells to maximise current through a given external resistance
questions.question: Six identical cells, each of emf \(2.0\text{ V}\) and internal resistance \(0.5\ \Omega\), are used with an external resistance \(R=3.0\ \Omega\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) In series the current is \(\dfrac{12}{3+3}=2.0\text{ A}\) and in parallel \(\dfrac{2}{3+0.083}\approx0.65\text{ A}\), so series gives more current when \(R\gg r\) while parallel is better when \(R\ll r\); the terminal voltage of a cell is \(V=E-Ir\) while it delivers current and \(V=E+Ir\) while it is being charged, and the short-circuit current of one cell is \(E/r=4\text{ A}\)
B) The terminal voltage of a cell always equals its emf
C) Parallel grouping always gives the largest current
D) While charging, the terminal voltage is \(E-Ir\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\text{series }2.0\text{ A},\ \text{parallel }\approx0.65\text{ A};\ V=E\mp Ir;\ I_{\text{sc}}=4\text{ A}\)
Given: \(E=2.0\text{ V},\ r=0.5\ \Omega,\ n=6,\ R=3.0\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{series: }I=\dfrac{nE}{R+nr};\ \text{parallel: }I=\dfrac{E}{R+r/n}\)
Step 1: \(\text{series: }\dfrac{12}{3+3}=2.0\text{ A}\)
Step 2: \(\text{parallel: }\dfrac{2}{3+0.0833}=0.649\text{ A}\)
Step 3: \(I_{\text{sc}}=\dfrac{E}{r}=\dfrac{2}{0.5}=4\text{ A}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{series beats parallel when }\frac{nE}{R+nr}>\frac{nE}{nR+r}\Leftrightarrow nR+r>R+nr\Leftrightarrow R>r\]
Check: \[\text{series: }V_{\text{terminal}}=12-2\times3=6\ \text{V}=IR=2\times3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{internal resistance drops part of the emf whenever current flows}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(V=E\text{ only when }I=0\); (C) \(\text{depends on }R\text{ vs }r\); (D) \(\text{charging gives }E+Ir\).
Key point: \(V=E-Ir\ (\text{discharge}),\ E+Ir\ (\text{charging});\ \text{series if }R>r\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the shunt needed to convert a galvanometer into an ammeter and the series resistance to convert it into a voltmeter, and why ammeters and voltmeters have low and high resistance
questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance \(50\ \Omega\) gives full-scale deflection at \(2.0\text{ mA}\). What shunt converts it into a 0–1 A ammeter, and what series resistance converts it into a 0–10 V voltmeter? Which statement about the meters is correct?
options: A) \(0.1\ \Omega\text{ in series};\ 4950\ \Omega\text{ in parallel}\)

B) \(\approx0.10\ \Omega\text{ in parallel};\ 4950\ \Omega\text{ in series};\ \text{the ammeter has very low resistance and is connected in series, the voltmeter very high resistance and is connected in parallel, so neither disturbs the circuit much; current sensitivity }NAB/k\text{ rises with turns and field}\)
C) \(50\ \Omega;\ 5000\ \Omega;\ \text{ammeter has high resistance}\)
D) \(500\ \Omega;\ 0.1\ \Omega;\ \text{voltmeter is connected in series}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(S\approx0.10\ \Omega\text{ (shunt)};\ R=4950\ \Omega\text{ (series)}\)
Given: \(G=50\ \Omega,\ I_g=2.0\times10^{-3}\text{ A}\)
Formula/Principle: \(S=\dfrac{I_gG}{I-I_g};\ R=\dfrac{V}{I_g}-G\)
Step 1: \(S=\dfrac{0.002\times50}{0.998}=0.1002\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(R=\dfrac{10}{0.002}-50=5000-50=4950\ \Omega\)
Step 3: \(R_{\text{ammeter}}=\dfrac{SG}{S+G}\approx0.1\ \Omega;\ R_{\text{voltmeter}}=5000\ \Omega\)
Worked derivation: \[I_gG=(I-I_g)S\ \ (\text{equal p.d. across galvanometer and shunt})\]
Check: \[I_g(G+R)=0.002\times5000=10\ \text{V}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the shunt carries most of the current, and the series resistor drops most of the voltage}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{connections swapped}\); (C) \(\text{values wrong; ammeter is low resistance}\); (D) \(\text{values swapped; voltmeter is in parallel}\).
Key point: \(S=I_gG/(I-I_g);\ R=V/I_g-G\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying Faraday's law to find the induced emf in a coil and using Lenz's law to explain magnetic braking of a magnet in a copper tube and the jumping ring experiment
questions.question: A 100-turn coil of area \(0.020\text{ m}^2\) is in a field that falls uniformly from \(0.50\text{ T}\) to zero in \(0.10\text{ s}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) The induced emf is \(0.10\text{ V}\); a magnet falls through a copper tube faster than through a plastic tube
B) No emf is induced because the field is decreasing

C) The induced emf is \(N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{100\times0.020\times0.50}{0.10}=10\text{ V}\), and by Lenz's law the induced current flows so as to oppose the decrease of flux; a magnet dropped through a copper tube falls slowly because eddy currents induced in the tube oppose its motion, and an aluminium ring on an iron-cored coil jumps when the current is switched on because the induced current in the ring repels the coil — both are consequences of energy conservation
D) The induced current always flows so as to increase the change in flux
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\varepsilon=10\text{ V};\ \text{Lenz's law explains the falling magnet and jumping ring}\)
Given: \(N=100,\ A=0.020\text{ m}^2,\ \Delta B=0.50\text{ T},\ \Delta t=0.10\text{ s}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt},\ \Phi=BA\)
Step 1: \(\Delta\Phi=0.020\times0.50=0.010\text{ Wb}\)
Step 2: \(\varepsilon=\dfrac{100\times0.010}{0.10}=10\text{ V}\)
Step 3: \(\text{current direction opposes the change: it tries to maintain the original flux}\)
Worked derivation: \[|\varepsilon|=N\frac{\Delta(BA)}{\Delta t}=NA\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}=100\times0.020\times5.0=10\ \text{V}\]
Check: \[\text{if the induced current aided the change, it would accelerate itself without limit, violating energy conservation}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{any change in flux induces an emf, and its direction always opposes that change}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{emf miscalculated; eddy currents slow the magnet}\); (B) \(\text{a decreasing flux also induces emf}\); (D) \(\text{Lenz's law says oppose}\).
Key point: \(\varepsilon=-N\,d\Phi/dt;\ \text{induced effects oppose the cause}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating peak emf of an AC generator from coil parameters, and current and turns ratios of an ideal step-down transformer, with the reason for high-voltage power transmission
questions.question: A generator coil has 100 turns of area \(0.10\text{ m}^2\) rotating at 50 rev s⁻¹ in a \(0.50\text{ T}\) field. Find the peak emf. An ideal transformer steps 2200 V down to 220 V and supplies 10 A to a load; find the turns ratio and primary current. Why is power transmitted at high voltage?
options: A) \(1570\text{ V};\ N_p:N_s=10:1;\ 1.0\text{ A};\ \text{for the same power a higher voltage means a smaller current, reducing }I^2R\text{ losses in the lines}\)
B) \(250\text{ V};\ 1:10;\ 100\text{ A};\ \text{high voltage increases current}\)
C) \(1570\text{ V};\ 10:1;\ 100\text{ A};\ \text{to make the wires thinner only}\)
D) \(5\text{ V};\ 1:1;\ 10\text{ A};\ \text{transformers work with DC}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\varepsilon_0\approx1570\text{ V};\ 10:1;\ I_p=1.0\text{ A}\)
Given: \(N=100,\ A=0.10\text{ m}^2,\ B=0.50\text{ T},\ \nu=50\text{ Hz};\ V_p=2200,\ V_s=220\text{ V},\ I_s=10\text{ A}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega;\ \dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}=\dfrac{I_p}{I_s}\)
Step 1: \(\omega=2\pi\times50=314\text{ rad s}^{-1}\Rightarrow\varepsilon_0=100\times0.50\times0.10\times314=1570\text{ V}\)
Step 2: \(N_p:N_s=2200:220=10:1\)
Step 3: \(I_p=I_s\times\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=10\times\tfrac1{10}=1.0\text{ A}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Phi=NBA\cos\omega t\Rightarrow\varepsilon=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=NBA\omega\sin\omega t\]
Check: \[V_pI_p=2200\times1=2200\ \text{W}=V_sI_s=220\times10\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{an ideal transformer conserves power, so stepping voltage down steps current up}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\omega\text{ omitted; ratio inverted}\); (C) \(I_p\text{ is smaller than }I_s\); (D) \(\text{values wrong; transformers need AC}\).
Key point: \(\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega;\ V_pI_p=V_sI_s\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the power and focal length of two thin lenses in contact, and interpreting the straight-line graph of 1/v against 1/u for a thin lens
questions.question: A convex lens of focal length \(20\text{ cm}\) is placed in contact with a concave lens of focal length \(30\text{ cm}\). Find the power and focal length of the combination. A student plots \(1/v\) against \(1/u\) (sign convention) for a single convex lens; what does the graph look like?
options: A) \(+8.3\text{ D};\ 12\text{ cm};\ \text{a parabola}\)
B) \(-1.67\text{ D};\ -60\text{ cm};\ \text{a straight line of slope }-1\)
C) \(+1.67\text{ D};\ 60\text{ cm (converging)};\ \text{a straight line of slope }+1\text{ whose intercept on the }1/v\text{ axis is }1/f\)
D) \(+1.67\text{ D};\ 50\text{ cm};\ \text{a rectangular hyperbola}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(P=+1.67\text{ D};\ f=60\text{ cm};\ \text{line of slope }1\text{, intercept }1/f\)
Given: \(f_1=+0.20\text{ m},\ f_2=-0.30\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=P_1+P_2,\ P=\dfrac1f\ (f\text{ in m});\ \dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f\)
Step 1: \(P_1=+5.0\text{ D},\ P_2=-3.33\text{ D}\)
Step 2: \(P=+1.67\text{ D}\Rightarrow f=\dfrac1{1.67}=0.60\text{ m}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac1u+\dfrac1f\Rightarrow\text{slope }1,\ \text{intercept }\dfrac1f\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac1F=\frac1{f_1}+\frac1{f_2}=\frac1{20}-\frac1{30}=\frac{1}{60}\ \text{cm}^{-1}\]
Check: \[F>0\text{ because the convex lens is stronger}\Rightarrow\text{converging}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{powers of thin lenses in contact add algebraically}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{added the magnitudes}\); (B) \(\text{sign wrong; slope is }+1\); (D) \(f=60\text{ cm};\ \text{graph is linear}\).
Key point: \(P=\sum P_i;\ 1/v=1/u+1/f\)

questions.sub_topic: Applying Einstein's photoelectric equation as energy conservation to find maximum kinetic energy, stopping potential, threshold wavelength and maximum electron speed, and the effect of intensity
questions.question: Light of wavelength \(400\text{ nm}\) falls on a metal of work function \(2.0\text{ eV}\) (\(hc=1240\text{ eV nm},\ m_e=9.1\times10^{-31}\text{ kg}\)). Find \(K_{\max}\), the stopping potential, the threshold wavelength and the maximum speed of photoelectrons. What happens when the intensity is doubled?
options: A) \(3.1\text{ eV};\ 3.1\text{ V};\ 400\text{ nm};\ 1.0\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1};\ K_{\max}\text{ doubles}\)

B) \(1.1\text{ eV};\ 1.1\text{ V};\ 620\text{ nm};\ 6.2\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1};\ K_{\max}\text{ and stopping potential unchanged, photocurrent doubles; emission is instantaneous and no electrons are emitted below the threshold frequency however intense the light}\)
C) \(5.1\text{ eV};\ 5.1\text{ V};\ 248\text{ nm};\ 1.3\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{current unchanged}\)
D) \(1.1\text{ eV};\ 2.2\text{ V};\ 310\text{ nm};\ 6.2\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{stopping potential doubles}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(K_{\max}=1.1\text{ eV};\ V_0=1.1\text{ V};\ \lambda_0=620\text{ nm};\ v_{\max}\approx6.2\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Given: \(\lambda=400\text{ nm},\ \phi_0=2.0\text{ eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(h\nu=\phi_0+K_{\max};\ eV_0=K_{\max};\ \lambda_0=\dfrac{hc}{\phi_0}\)
Step 1: \(h\nu=\dfrac{1240}{400}=3.1\text{ eV}\Rightarrow K_{\max}=1.1\text{ eV},\ V_0=1.1\text{ V}\)
Step 2: \(\lambda_0=\dfrac{1240}{2.0}=620\text{ nm}\)
Step 3: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1.1\times1.6\times10^{-19}}{9.1\times10^{-31}}}=\sqrt{3.87\times10^{11}}\approx6.2\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[\underbrace{h\nu}_{\text{photon energy}}=\underbrace{\phi_0}_{\text{to free the electron}}+\underbrace{\tfrac12mv_{\max}^2}_{\text{left as kinetic energy}}\]
Check: \[\frac{hc}{\lambda_0}=\phi_0=2.0\ \text{eV};\ 3.1-2.0=1.1\ \text{eV}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each electron absorbs one photon, so photon energy (frequency) fixes }K_{\max}\text{ while intensity fixes the number of electrons}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\phi_0\text{ not subtracted; intensity does not raise }K_{\max}\); (C) \(\phi_0\text{ added}\); (D) \(eV_0=K_{\max};\ \lambda_0=620\text{ nm}\).
Key point: \(K_{\max}=h\nu-\phi_0;\ \text{intensity}\to\text{current only}\)
